Ideas expressed in the piece
The column contends that California’s gubernatorial recall process has become a costly outlet for partisan grievance, pointing to the 2021 effort against Gov. Gavin Newsom as an expensive, largely redundant re-litigation of the 2018 election rather than a meaningful exercise in accountability [5] (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/op-ed/article253864413.html) . It suggests that such recalls siphon public money and attention from governance while merely confirming outcomes voters had already endorsed [5] (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/op-ed/article253864413.html) .
The article argues that the core structural flaw in California’s recall rules is the two-question ballot, which allows voters to remove an incumbent by majority vote while simultaneously electing a replacement who may win with only a small plurality [2] (https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2022-02-13/editorial-californias-recall-rules-could-let-a-loser-win-its-time-to-change-that) [6] (https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2024-03-19/editorial-newsom-recall-still-not-fixed-undemocratic-rules) [11] (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-08-16/skelton-recall-constitutionality-newsom-california-governor) . It notes that in a crowded field this can produce a scenario where a governor receives far more votes than the successor yet still loses office, a result critics in other commentaries have labeled undemocratic and potentially unconstitutional [2] (https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2022-02-13/editorial-californias-recall-rules-could-let-a-loser-win-its-time-to-change-that) [6] (https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2024-03-19/editorial-newsom-recall-still-not-fixed-undemocratic-rules) [11] (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-08-16/skelton-recall-constitutionality-newsom-california-governor) .
Building on that critique, the piece supports Proposition 5, a legislatively referred constitutional amendment on the November 2026 ballot that would eliminate the simultaneous successor election and ask a single yes-or-no question about recalling the incumbent [4] (https://fullertonobserver.com/2026/08/15/california-proposition-5-2026-eliminating-the-successor-election-in-state-officer-recalls/) [7] (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316600442.html) [12] (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-5/) . It explains that, under the measure, a recalled governor’s seat would be filled either by the lieutenant governor for the remainder of the term or, when the recall occurs early in a term, by a special election in which the winner must secure a majority, with a runoff if necessary, thereby ensuring the replacement takes office with broader voter support [4] (https://fullertonobserver.com/2026/08/15/california-proposition-5-2026-eliminating-the-successor-election-in-state-officer-recalls/) [7] (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316600442.html) [12] (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-5/) .
The column further maintains that California’s signature threshold for initiating a gubernatorial recall—12% of votes cast in the previous governor’s race, roughly 1.5 million signatures in Newsom’s case—makes it too easy for a relatively small, motivated minority to force a statewide election [9] (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/prior-elections/statewide-election-results/2021-ca-gov-recall/newsom-recall-faqs) [10] (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article250011419.html) . It argues that the bar should be higher and that grounds for recall should be limited to serious misconduct such as corruption or criminal conviction, echoing concerns in oversight reports that the current open-ended standard invites overuse and abuse of the process [1] (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/FactSheet266.pdf) [8] (https://lhc.ca.gov/report/reforming-recall/) [10] (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article250011419.html) .
In addition, the piece suggests that the recall has drifted from its Progressive-era good-government roots into a tool for “bad actors” who can target officials they simply dislike and potentially install successors lacking majority support [1] (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/FactSheet266.pdf) [8] (https://lhc.ca.gov/report/reforming-recall/) . It cites reform recommendations from the Little Hoover Commission, which has urged changes such as raising the signature requirement and restricting recall timing, as evidence that independent watchdogs also see the existing framework as vulnerable to manipulation and in need of modernization [1] (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/FactSheet266.pdf) [8] (https://lhc.ca.gov/report/reforming-recall/) .
Different views on the topic
A law review article argues that California’s recall system is not overpowered and, in fact, functions much as its Progressive-era designers intended: as a difficult but potent “voter weapon” to menace and remove public officials when necessary [3] (https://digitalcommons.law.scu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2938&context=lawreview) . It notes that from 1911 to 2021, 179 recall petitions were filed against state officials, but only 11 qualified for the ballot and just six succeeded, a record the piece uses to contend that recalls are already rare and that fears of rampant abuse are overstated [3] (https://digitalcommons.law.scu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2938&context=lawreview) .
While sharing concerns about undemocratic outcomes, some reform advocates favor a different structural fix than Proposition 5, proposing a “snap” special recall election in which the incumbent appears on the ballot alongside all challengers rather than leaving the office temporarily vacant [8] (https://lhc.ca.gov/report/reforming-recall/) . The Little Hoover Commission, for example, recommends replacing the two-part ballot with such a system and adjusting the signature requirement to 10% of registered voters, arguing that this approach both raises the bar for launching a recall and ensures that any successor must defeat the incumbent directly in a single election [1] (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/FactSheet266.pdf) [8] (https://lhc.ca.gov/report/reforming-recall/) .
The law review piece also emphasizes the historical role of the recall as a central Progressive innovation that gives voters a direct tool to check officials between regular election cycles, and it warns that sweeping restrictions on who can initiate recalls or on permissible reasons could blunt that instrument of accountability [3] (https://digitalcommons.law.scu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2938&context=lawreview) . By stressing that recall attempts are frequently filed but rarely successful, the article suggests that the existing hurdles already filter out frivolous efforts and that tightening the rules further could unduly insulate incumbents from public pressure [3] (https://digitalcommons.law.scu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2938&context=lawreview) .

The column further maintains that California’s signature threshold for initiating a gubernatorial recall—12% of votes cast in the previous governor’s race, roughly 1.5 million signatures in Newsom’s case—makes it too easy for a relatively small, motivated minority to force a statewide election [9] (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/prior-elections/statewide-election-results/2021-ca-gov-recall/newsom-recall-faqs) [10] (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article250011419.html) . It argues that the bar should be higher and that grounds for recall should be limited to serious misconduct such as corruption or criminal conviction, echoing concerns in oversight reports that the current open-ended standard invites overuse and abuse of the process [1] (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/FactSheet266.pdf) [8] (https://lhc.ca.gov/report/reforming-recall/) [10] (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article250011419.html) .
In addition, the piece suggests that the recall has drifted from its Progressive-era good-government roots into a tool for “bad actors” who can target officials they simply dislike and potentially install successors lacking majority support [1] (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/FactSheet266.pdf) [8] (https://lhc.ca.gov/report/reforming-recall/) . It cites reform recommendations from the Little Hoover Commission, which has urged changes such as raising the signature requirement and restricting recall timing, as evidence that independent watchdogs also see the existing framework as vulnerable to manipulation and in need of modernization [1] (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/FactSheet266.pdf) [8] (https://lhc.ca.gov/report/reforming-recall/) .
Different views on the topic
A law review article argues that California’s recall system is not overpowered and, in fact, functions much as its Progressive-era designers intended: as a difficult but potent “voter weapon” to menace and remove public officials when necessary [3] (https://digitalcommons.law.scu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2938&context=lawreview) . It notes that from 1911 to 2021, 179 recall petitions were filed against state officials, but only 11 qualified for the ballot and just six succeeded, a record the piece uses to contend that recalls are already rare and that fears of rampant abuse are overstated [3] (https://digitalcommons.law.scu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2938&context=lawreview) .
While sharing concerns about undemocratic outcomes, some reform advocates favor a different structural fix than Proposition 5, proposing a “snap” special recall election in which the incumbent appears on the ballot alongside all challengers rather than leaving the office temporarily vacant [8] (https://lhc.ca.gov/report/reforming-recall/) . The Little Hoover Commission, for example, recommends replacing the two-part ballot with such a system and adjusting the signature requirement to 10% of registered voters, arguing that this approach both raises the bar for launching a recall and ensures that any successor must defeat the incumbent directly in a single election [1] (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/FactSheet266.pdf) [8] (https://lhc.ca.gov/report/reforming-recall/) .
The law review piece also emphasizes the historical role of the recall as a central Progressive innovation that gives voters a direct tool to check officials between regular election cycles, and it warns that sweeping restrictions on who can initiate recalls or on permissible reasons could blunt that instrument of accountability [3] (https://digitalcommons.law.scu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2938&context=lawreview) . By stressing that recall attempts are frequently filed but rarely successful, the article suggests that the existing hurdles already filter out frivolous efforts and that tightening the rules further could unduly insulate incumbents from public pressure [3] (https://digitalcommons.law.scu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2938&context=lawreview) .

# Proposition 5: Statewide Officers
## Proposition 5: Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
### Summary
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process.
Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled.
If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law.
Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor.
If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.
...

YES: A “yes” vote supports changing California’s recall process so voters would decide only whether to remove an official, with the vacancy filled later under state law.
A recalled official could run again, and the Lieutenant Governor would generally replace a recalled Governor.
NO: A “no” vote supports keeping the current recall process, in which voters decide whether to remove an official and simultaneously vote on who should replace that official if the recall succeeds.

Ideas expressed in the piece
The column contends that California’s gubernatorial recall process has become a costly outlet for partisan grievance, pointing to the 2021 effort against Gov. Gavin Newsom as an expensive, largely redundant re-litigation of the 2018 election rather than a meaningful exercise in accountability [5] (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/op-ed/article253864413.html) . It suggests that such recalls siphon public money and attention from governance while merely confirming outcomes voters had already endorsed [5] (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/op-ed/article253864413.html) .
The article argues that the core structural flaw in California’s recall rules is the two-question ballot, which allows voters to remove an incumbent by majority vote while simultaneously electing a replacement who may win with only a small plurality [2] (https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2022-02-13/editorial-californias-recall-rules-could-let-a-loser-win-its-time-to-change-that) [6] (https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2024-03-19/editorial-newsom-recall-still-not-fixed-undemocratic-rules) [11] (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-08-16/skelton-recall-constitutionality-newsom-california-governor) . It notes that in a crowded field this can produce a scenario where a governor receives far more votes than the successor yet still loses office, a result critics in other commentaries have labeled undemocratic and potentially unconstitutional [2] (https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2022-02-13/editorial-californias-recall-rules-could-let-a-loser-win-its-time-to-change-that) [6] (https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2024-03-19/editorial-newsom-recall-still-not-fixed-undemocratic-rules) [11] (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-08-16/skelton-recall-constitutionality-newsom-california-governor) .
Building on that critique, the piece supports Proposition 5, a legislatively referred constitutional amendment on the November 2026 ballot that would eliminate the simultaneous successor election and ask a single yes-or-no question about recalling the incumbent [4] (https://fullertonobserver.com/2026/08/15/california-proposition-5-2026-eliminating-the-successor-election-in-state-officer-recalls/) [7] (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316600442.html) [12] (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-5/) . It explains that, under the measure, a recalled governor’s seat would be filled either by the lieutenant governor for the remainder of the term or, when the recall occurs early in a term, by a special election in which the winner must secure a majority, with a runoff if necessary, thereby ensuring the replacement takes office with broader voter support [4] (https://fullertonobserver.com/2026/08/15/california-proposition-5-2026-eliminating-the-successor-election-in-state-officer-recalls/) [7] (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316600442.html) [12] (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-5/) .
The column further maintains that California’s signature threshold for initiating a gubernatorial recall—12% of votes cast in the previous governor’s race, roughly 1.5 million signatures in Newsom’s case—makes it too easy for a relatively small, motivated minority to force a statewide election [9] (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/prior-elections/statewide-election-results/2021-ca-gov-recall/newsom-recall-faqs) [10] (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article250011419.html) . It argues that the bar should be higher and that grounds for recall should be limited to serious misconduct such as corruption or criminal conviction, echoing concerns in oversight reports that the current open-ended standard invites overuse and abuse of the process [1] (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/FactSheet266.pdf) [8] (https://lhc.ca.gov/report/reforming-recall/) [10] (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article250011419.html) .
In addition, the piece suggests that the recall has drifted from its Progressive-era good-government roots into a tool for “bad actors” who can target officials they simply dislike and potentially install successors lacking majority support [1] (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/FactSheet266.pdf) [8] (https://lhc.ca.gov/report/reforming-recall/) . It cites reform recommendations from the Little Hoover Commission, which has urged changes such as raising the signature requirement and restricting recall timing, as evidence that independent watchdogs also see the existing framework as vulnerable to manipulation and in need of modernization [1] (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/FactSheet266.pdf) [8] (https://lhc.ca.gov/report/reforming-recall/) .
Different views on the topic
A law review article argues that California’s recall system is not overpowered and, in fact, functions much as its Progressive-era designers intended: as a difficult but potent “voter weapon” to menace and remove public officials when necessary [3] (https://digitalcommons.law.scu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2938&context=lawreview) . It notes that from 1911 to 2021, 179 recall petitions were filed against state officials, but only 11 qualified for the ballot and just six succeeded, a record the piece uses to contend that recalls are already rare and that fears of rampant abuse are overstated [3] (https://digitalcommons.law.scu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2938&context=lawreview) .
While sharing concerns about undemocratic outcomes, some reform advocates favor a different structural fix than Proposition 5, proposing a “snap” special recall election in which the incumbent appears on the ballot alongside all challengers rather than leaving the office temporarily vacant [8] (https://lhc.ca.gov/report/reforming-recall/) . The Little Hoover Commission, for example, recommends replacing the two-part ballot with such a system and adjusting the signature requirement to 10% of registered voters, arguing that this approach both raises the bar for launching a recall and ensures that any successor must defeat the incumbent directly in a single election [1] (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/FactSheet266.pdf) [8] (https://lhc.ca.gov/report/reforming-recall/) .
The law review piece also emphasizes the historical role of the recall as a central Progressive innovation that gives voters a direct tool to check officials between regular election cycles, and it warns that sweeping restrictions on who can initiate recalls or on permissible reasons could blunt that instrument of accountability [3] (https://digitalcommons.law.scu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2938&context=lawreview) . By stressing that recall attempts are frequently filed but rarely successful, the article suggests that the existing hurdles already filter out frivolous efforts and that tightening the rules further could unduly insulate incumbents from public pressure [3] (https://digitalcommons.law.scu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2938&context=lawreview) .

# Proposition 5: Statewide Officers
## Proposition 5: Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
### Summary
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process.
Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled.
If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law.
Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor.
If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.
...
### What your vote means

WWW.LHC.CA.GOVLITTLE HOOVER COMMISSIONFact Sheet: Addressing Weaknesses in
California’s Recall System
Contact: LittleHoover@lhc.ca.gov
The attempted recall of Governor Gavin
Newsom, which produced California’s second
gubernatorial recall election in less than 20
years, focused attention on the recall process
and on whether that system requires reform.
As California’s independent oversight agency,
the Little Hoover Commission launched a
study in 2021-2022 to consider whether
the state’s system for recalling state office-
holders should be changed, and if so, how.
The Commission concluded that the recall
system should be retained, both because it
is substantively valuable—voters should be
able to fire an elected official mid-term—and
because it is overwhelmingly popular with
voters.
Yet substantial changes are needed in
California’s recall process. Current recall
procedures breed the possibility of an
undemocratic outcome, since they allow a
replacement candidate to win office while
receiving fewer votes than the incumbent.
There is also concern that the recall is subject
to potential overuse or abuse.
In its 2022 report, Reforming the Recall, the
Commission recommends that California make two
key changes to its recall system:
◊ Adjust the signature requirement for recalling
statewide office-holders from 12 percent of
the vote in the last election for the office to 10
percent of registered voters, thereby increasing
the number of signatures necessary to initiate
a recall election and creating a more stable
signature threshold.
◊ Replace the existing two-part recall ballot with
a “snap” special election in which the official
targeted for recall is placed on the ballot with all
replacement candidates. This would ensure that
no official is recalled and replaced by a successor
who receives fewer votes.
The Commission also identified several smaller,
procedural changes that would give elections officials
more time to administer elections and provide
greater clarity around the recall process:
◊ Extend the timeframe for conducting recall
elections to no less than 88 days and no more
than 125 days from certification of the recall
petition as sufficient.
◊ Prohibit the initiation of recall proceedings
against state office-holders during the first 90
days and the last six months of their term in
office.
◊ Review recall replacement procedures to
determine which nomination standard is most
appropriate for replacement candidates, and
establish in statute which one ought to be used.
These steps will strengthen the recall system by
improving administration of the recall and better
balancing voters’ right to recall officials with
protection for electoral integrity and democratic
principles.
ADDITIONAL IMPLEMENTATION
◊ SCA 3 (Allen), 2020: Would have eliminated the
first recall ballot question and automatically
placed the official subject to recall on the ballot
as a candidate for the office.
Last updated: January 2023

Proposition 5: Will California’s Boa Constrictor Strike Again?
One seemingly innocent ballot initiative which would change California’s recall process—if voters approve it, hasta la vista, future governators (https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/november-17/the-terminator-becomes-the-governator-of-california)!—fits into a pattern of repeat efforts to guarantee that the Golden State remains under one-party, one-mentality dominance.
Thursday, October 8, 2026
5
min read
By:
Bill Whalen (https://www.hoover.org/profiles/bill-whalen) ,
Proposition 5: Will California’s Boa Constrictor Strike Again?
By:
Bill Whalen (https://www.hoover.org/profiles/bill-whalen)

California Decides
One doesn’t need a degree in ophiology (https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/ophiology) to know that some boas achieve their goals not by venom but instead by slowly constricting their prey’s circulatory system until vital organs shut down.
At least, that’s one way to explain how one political party has dominated the California landscape this century: for the better part of the last two decades, a slow but steady constriction of the loyal opposition’s ability to affect political and policy outcomes.
Case in point: this year’s Proposition 5 (https://www.hoover.org/proposition-lab-proposition-5), one of fourteen measures on California’s November slate of ballot initiatives.
At first glance, Proposition 5 seems innocent enough, or so its official summary assures us: “ Under current law, voters elect replacement candidates at the same time as the recall election. This measure instead fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment.”
And how exactly would that work?
Again, the summary’s words:
“If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor becomes Governor for the remainder of the term or until a successor is elected”;
“for all other recalled officers, the office will remain vacant until filled by a subsequent special election or appointment as specified in existing law”;
“a recalled officer may be a candidate in a special election to fill the office.”
So how does this constitute yet another slow-but-certain “constriction”? Simple. Republicans have failed spectacularly at winning California statewide offices. (In this century, excluding the 2003 recall special election, only two GOP wins occurred in fifty-one runs for state constitutional and US Senate offices.) But there’s always been a back door to the governor’s office: the recall process.
Or so California learned when Arnold Schwarzenegger became the Golden State’s thirty-eighth governor by virtue of a recall election (https://www.politico.com/story/2017/10/07/schwarzenegger-elected-californias-governor-oct-7-2003-243512) — twenty-three years ago this week — that ousted the incumbent Democrat, Gray Davis. For Arnold, it was a two-month “fun run” — assuming the candidate enjoyed dropping wrecking balls on junkers (https://www.theguardian.com/world/2003/oct/04/usa.duncancampbell) to underscore his opposition to a “car tax” — that allowed the Republican contender to avoid a contentious GOP primary and prolonged questions about his conservative bona fides (https://californiahealthline.org/morning-breakout/schwarzenegger-social-positions-exhibit-differences-with-republican-party/).
But if voters approve Prop 5, that “back door” for a non-Democratic governor vanishes. As such, it’s just one more way in which a party that controls every statewide office, as well as supermajorities in both legislative chambers, maintains its dominance.
How else has the constrictor gone about its business in California?
Here are five examples, in reverse chronological order.
Proposition 50 . Yes, California Gov. Gavin Newsom will tell you that the ballot measure redrawing California’s congressional districts (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_50,_Use_of_Legislative_Congressional_Redistricting_Map_Amendment_(2025)) and approved by voters last November was in response to the Republican congressional gerrymander in Texas (https://redistricting.capitol.texas.gov/). And he’ll assure you it’s but a temporary step as it applies to congressional elections through 2030.
What Proposition 50 did, in the near term, was target five incumbent congressional Republicans (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-seats-would-democrats-gain-under-californias-mid-decade-redistricting-plan/). (One of them, Rep. Kevin Kiley, is now running as an independent (https://abc7news.com/post/california-rep-kevin-kiley-says-hes-leaving-republican-party-will-serve-independent/18699488/) in California’s less GOP-friendly 6th Congressional District, which stretches from the foothills of Placer County to Sacramento.)
But in the longer term, Proposition 50 “constricts” in this regard: By taking redistricting authority away from a nonpartisan, independent commission (https://wedrawthelines.ca.gov/about-us/) and instead allowing the Democratic-controlled Legislature to do the political cartography, it sets the precedent for future attempts to whittle away at the California GOP’s numbers in the US House of Representatives.
Universal Vote-By-Mail . Six years ago, California election officials rightly worried that voters going to polls amid a pandemic could trigger a superspreader event (https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2021/09/27/california-will-now-mail-ballots-voters-all-elections-permanent-extension-pandemic-era-practice/). The solution: Send a mail-in ballot to every registered regular voter, whether they asked for it or not.
A year later, Newsom signed 2021’s Assembly Bill 37 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220AB37) making California a permanent voter-by-mail state, tweeting in Trumpian fashion (https://x.com/GavinNewsom/status/1442573769906688001): “ BREAKING: California is now PERMANENTLY a vote-by-mail state. Because we believe in making voting EASIER and for every voice to be heard.”
What California’s governor conveniently omitted: voter-registration mathematics. Democrats in the Golden State outnumber Republicans by nearly a two-to-one margin (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ror/60day-gen-2026/historical-reg-stats.pdf) (it’s a twenty-point gap, as opposed to the eight-point divide between Republicans and Democrats that Schwarzenegger faced when running for reelection twenty years ago). In addition to the advanced degree in snake-handling, one doesn’t need a math doctorate to know that more ballots handed to registered Democrats means fewer chances of non-Democratic candidates or policies prevailing.
Primary Initiatives Banned . In every election cycle, California’s secretary of state publishes a thoughtful Voter Information Guide (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/) that’s mailed to all registered voters. In this election, the guide includes sixty-five pages of insight and arguments (both pro and con) devoted to fourteen ballot measures.
If you consider that information overload and would like to file a complaint, former Gov. Jerry Brown would be a good place to start.
In 2011, his first year back at the same job he held three decades earlier, Brown signed SB 202 (https://archive.nytimes.com/www.nytimes.com/gwire/2011/10/10/10greenwire-new-calif-ballot-law-seen-as-boon-to-liberal-i-42681.html?pagewanted=1), which banned voter-driven initiatives from future Golden State primary ballots. At the time, Brown tried to sell the measure as an act of good government—and good faith. “There are dramatically more voters at a general rather than a primary election," the governor’s signing statement read. “The idea of direct democracy is to involve as many voters as possible. This bill accomplishes that objective."
What Brown could have added: Moving all voter initiatives to the general election improved the odds of killing off right-leading ideas, as conservatives tend to have a larger presence in lower-turnout primaries.
Indeed, in the following year’s election, Brown’s move may have prevented “paycheck protection” (banning the use of union dues as political contributions to state and local candidates) from becoming the law of the land.
How so?
In 2012, paycheck protection was offered in the form of Proposition 32 (https://vigarchive.sos.ca.gov/2012/general/propositions/32/). Given the opportunity, the backers of that measure likely would have placed it on the ballot believing that it would benefit from the Republican primary calendar (Mitt Romney clinched the GOP nomination less than a week before California voted (https://www.politico.com/story/2012/05/mitt-clinches-gop-presidential-nod-076845)). Rare for California, the state witnessed a Republican enthusiasm gap. (Despite 2.1 million more registered Democrats than Republicans, the Democratic presidential candidates competing in California’s primary received only 150,000 more votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2012-primary/pdf/2012-complete-sov.pdf) than the GOP). Instead, Proposition 32 was relegated to the November ballot, where it received only 43.4 percent.
Despite this constricting move, right-of-center and free-market ideas can still prevail in the form of ballot initiatives—but maybe not that many initiatives if the going rate for victory is at least $200 million (https://www.sfexaminer.com/news/politics/billionaire-tax-fight-has-become-200m-battle/article_31b8898d-bb5a-4ff5-97a0-5921537adea6.html).
Majority Budgets . In the same 2010 election that returned Jerry Brown to the governor’s office, California voters sent a message to a legislature fresh off a three-month budgetary stalemate (https://www.bbc.com/news/world-us-canada-11458248) with Schwarzenegger: The next time the budget is delayed, you won’t get paid until you do your job.
Also a part of Proposition 25 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_25,_Simple_Majority_Vote_to_Enact_State_Budget_Amendment_(2010)), which made that salary-docking threat: lowering the vote requirement for each house of the legislature to pass a budget bill from two-thirds to a simple majority. (California, at the time, was one of only three states with the two-thirds requirement.)
The constriction was none too subtle. With Democrats firmly in control of the legislature when voters approved Proposition 25, but lacking supermajorities in either chamber, the constitutional tweak immediately made legislative Republicans irrelevant when charting California’s fiscal course—an irrelevancy that continues to this day.
Open Primaries . Proposition 14 wasn't California's only experiment in making democracy work to one party's advantage. Also on the ballot in November 2010 was Proposition 14 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_14,_Top-Two_Primaries_Amendment_(June_2010)), which offered a new “top two” primary system that advanced the lead two vote getters to the general election regardless of political affiliation.
Proponents of the ballot measure also talked about future primaries producing a new California politician (at the time, the political prognosticator Nate Silver predicted a future wave of New England-style moderates in the Golden State (https://web.archive.org/web/20140207043720/http:/www.fivethirtyeight.com/2009/02/land-of-thousand-liebermans.html)).
But what went overlooked at the time: Proposition 14 didn’t allow third parties access to the November ballot unless they finished first or second in the primary.
The constriction: keeping third-party candidates off the November ballot also keeps disgruntled Democrats and independents (currently breaking Democratic at a two-to-one rate (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/08s5x10r) in this year’s governor’s race) from leaving the flock.
A crippling blow it’s not. Third-party contenders accounted for only 5.3 percent of the vote (https://ballotpedia.org/California_gubernatorial_election,_2010) the last time California didn’t limit the gubernatorial choices to two candidates—Republican Meg Whitman still losing by nearly 13 points. But in 2002, four third-party candidates received a collective 10.3 percent of the November vote (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2002-general/ssov/gov-sum.pdf)—one of the reasons Republican Bill Simon lost by only five points.
About that 2002 election in California: For the first time ever (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/California-GOP-trying-to-make-sense-of-Democrats-2774055.php), Democrats won every statewide constitutional office, maintained their legislature dominance, and picked up a congressional seat. And 2026 likely offers more of the same—maybe more congressional pickups if the Proposition 50 gerrymander pans out.
California political outcomes seem little different nearly a quarter of a century later: talk about a long squeeze.

Proposition 5: Will California’s Boa Constrictor Strike Again?
One seemingly innocent ballot initiative which would change California’s recall process—if voters approve it, hasta la vista, future governators (https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/november-17/the-terminator-becomes-the-governator-of-california)!—fits into a pattern of repeat efforts to guarantee that the Golden State remains under one-party, one-mentality dominance.

California Decides
One doesn’t need a degree in ophiology (https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/ophiology) to know that some boas achieve their goals not by venom but instead by slowly constricting their prey’s circulatory system until vital organs shut down.
At least, that’s one way to explain how one political party has dominated the California landscape this century: for the better part of the last two decades, a slow but steady constriction of the loyal opposition’s ability to affect political and policy outcomes.
Case in point: this year’s Proposition 5 (https://www.hoover.org/proposition-lab-proposition-5), one of fourteen measures on California’s November slate of ballot initiatives.
At first glance, Proposition 5 seems innocent enough, or so its official summary assures us: “ Under current law, voters elect replacement candidates at the same time as the recall election. This measure instead fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment.”
And how exactly would that work?
Again, the summary’s words:
“If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor becomes Governor for the remainder of the term or until a successor is elected”;
“for all other recalled officers, the office will remain vacant until filled by a subsequent special election or appointment as specified in existing law”;
“a recalled officer may be a candidate in a special election to fill the office.”
So how does this constitute yet another slow-but-certain “constriction”? Simple. Republicans have failed spectacularly at winning California statewide offices. (In this century, excluding the 2003 recall special election, only two GOP wins occurred in fifty-one runs for state constitutional and US Senate offices.) But there’s always been a back door to the governor’s office: the recall process.
Or so California learned when Arnold Schwarzenegger became the Golden State’s thirty-eighth governor by virtue of a recall election (https://www.politico.com/story/2017/10/07/schwarzenegger-elected-californias-governor-oct-7-2003-243512) — twenty-three years ago this week — that ousted the incumbent Democrat, Gray Davis. For Arnold, it was a two-month “fun run” — assuming the candidate enjoyed dropping wrecking balls on junkers (https://www.theguardian.com/world/2003/oct/04/usa.duncancampbell) to underscore his opposition to a “car tax” — that allowed the Republican contender to avoid a contentious GOP primary and prolonged questions about his conservative bona fides (https://californiahealthline.org/morning-breakout/schwarzenegger-social-positions-exhibit-differences-with-republican-party/).
But if voters approve Prop 5, that “back door” for a non-Democratic governor vanishes. As such, it’s just one more way in which a party that controls every statewide office, as well as supermajorities in both legislative chambers, maintains its dominance.
How else has the constrictor gone about its business in California?
Here are five examples, in reverse chronological order.
Proposition 50 . Yes, California Gov. Gavin Newsom will tell you that the ballot measure redrawing California’s congressional districts (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_50,_Use_of_Legislative_Congressional_Redistricting_Map_Amendment_(2025)) and approved by voters last November was in response to the Republican congressional gerrymander in Texas (https://redistricting.capitol.texas.gov/). And he’ll assure you it’s but a temporary step as it applies to congressional elections through 2030.
What Proposition 50 did, in the near term, was target five incumbent congressional Republicans (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-seats-would-democrats-gain-under-californias-mid-decade-redistricting-plan/). (One of them, Rep. Kevin Kiley, is now running as an independent (https://abc7news.com/post/california-rep-kevin-kiley-says-hes-leaving-republican-party-will-serve-independent/18699488/) in California’s less GOP-friendly 6th Congressional District, which stretches from the foothills of Placer County to Sacramento.)
But in the longer term, Proposition 50 “constricts” in this regard: By taking redistricting authority away from a nonpartisan, independent commission (https://wedrawthelines.ca.gov/about-us/) and instead allowing the Democratic-controlled Legislature to do the political cartography, it sets the precedent for future attempts to whittle away at the California GOP’s numbers in the US House of Representatives.
Universal Vote-By-Mail . Six years ago, California election officials rightly worried that voters going to polls amid a pandemic could trigger a superspreader event (https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2021/09/27/california-will-now-mail-ballots-voters-all-elections-permanent-extension-pandemic-era-practice/). The solution: Send a mail-in ballot to every registered regular voter, whether they asked for it or not.
A year later, Newsom signed 2021’s Assembly Bill 37 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220AB37) making California a permanent voter-by-mail state, tweeting in Trumpian fashion (https://x.com/GavinNewsom/status/1442573769906688001): “ BREAKING: California is now PERMANENTLY a vote-by-mail state. Because we believe in making voting EASIER and for every voice to be heard.”
What California’s governor conveniently omitted: voter-registration mathematics. Democrats in the Golden State outnumber Republicans by nearly a two-to-one margin (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ror/60day-gen-2026/historical-reg-stats.pdf) (it’s a twenty-point gap, as opposed to the eight-point divide between Republicans and Democrats that Schwarzenegger faced when running for reelection twenty years ago). In addition to the advanced degree in snake-handling, one doesn’t need a math doctorate to know that more ballots handed to registered Democrats means fewer chances of non-Democratic candidates or policies prevailing.
Primary Initiatives Banned . In every election cycle, California’s secretary of state publishes a thoughtful Voter Information Guide (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/) that’s mailed to all registered voters. In this election, the guide includes sixty-five pages of insight and arguments (both pro and con) devoted to fourteen ballot measures.
If you consider that information overload and would like to file a complaint, former Gov. Jerry Brown would be a good place to start.
In 2011, his first year back at the same job he held three decades earlier, Brown signed SB 202 (https://archive.nytimes.com/www.nytimes.com/gwire/2011/10/10/10greenwire-new-calif-ballot-law-seen-as-boon-to-liberal-i-42681.html?pagewanted=1), which banned voter-driven initiatives from future Golden State primary ballots. At the time, Brown tried to sell the measure as an act of good government—and good faith. “There are dramatically more voters at a general rather than a primary election," the governor’s signing statement read. “The idea of direct democracy is to involve as many voters as possible. This bill accomplishes that objective."
What Brown could have added: Moving all voter initiatives to the general election improved the odds of killing off right-leading ideas, as conservatives tend to have a larger presence in lower-turnout primaries.
Indeed, in the following year’s election, Brown’s move may have prevented “paycheck protection” (banning the use of union dues as political contributions to state and local candidates) from becoming the law of the land.
How so?
In 2012, paycheck protection was offered in the form of Proposition 32 (https://vigarchive.sos.ca.gov/2012/general/propositions/32/). Given the opportunity, the backers of that measure likely would have placed it on the ballot believing that it would benefit from the Republican primary calendar (Mitt Romney clinched the GOP nomination less than a week before California voted (https://www.politico.com/story/2012/05/mitt-clinches-gop-presidential-nod-076845)). Rare for California, the state witnessed a Republican enthusiasm gap. (Despite 2.1 million more registered Democrats than Republicans, the Democratic presidential candidates competing in California’s primary received only 150,000 more votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2012-primary/pdf/2012-complete-sov.pdf) than the GOP). Instead, Proposition 32 was relegated to the November ballot, where it received only 43.4 percent.
Despite this constricting move, right-of-center and free-market ideas can still prevail in the form of ballot initiatives—but maybe not that many initiatives if the going rate for victory is at least $200 million (https://www.sfexaminer.com/news/politics/billionaire-tax-fight-has-become-200m-battle/article_31b8898d-bb5a-4ff5-97a0-5921537adea6.html).
Majority Budgets . In the same 2010 election that returned Jerry Brown to the governor’s office, California voters sent a message to a legislature fresh off a three-month budgetary stalemate (https://www.bbc.com/news/world-us-canada-11458248) with Schwarzenegger: The next time the budget is delayed, you won’t get paid until you do your job.
Also a part of Proposition 25 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_25,_Simple_Majority_Vote_to_Enact_State_Budget_Amendment_(2010)), which made that salary-docking threat: lowering the vote requirement for each house of the legislature to pass a budget bill from two-thirds to a simple majority. (California, at the time, was one of only three states with the two-thirds requirement.)
The constriction was none too subtle. With Democrats firmly in control of the legislature when voters approved Proposition 25, but lacking supermajorities in either chamber, the constitutional tweak immediately made legislative Republicans irrelevant when charting California’s fiscal course—an irrelevancy that continues to this day.
Open Primaries . Proposition 14 wasn't California's only experiment in making democracy work to one party's advantage. Also on the ballot in November 2010 was Proposition 14 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_14,_Top-Two_Primaries_Amendment_(June_2010)), which offered a new “top two” primary system that advanced the lead two vote getters to the general election regardless of political affiliation.
Proponents of the ballot measure also talked about future primaries producing a new California politician (at the time, the political prognosticator Nate Silver predicted a future wave of New England-style moderates in the Golden State (https://web.archive.org/web/20140207043720/http:/www.fivethirtyeight.com/2009/02/land-of-thousand-liebermans.html)).
But what went overlooked at the time: Proposition 14 didn’t allow third parties access to the November ballot unless they finished first or second in the primary.
The constriction: keeping third-party candidates off the November ballot also keeps disgruntled Democrats and independents (currently breaking Democratic at a two-to-one rate (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/08s5x10r) in this year’s governor’s race) from leaving the flock.
A crippling blow it’s not. Third-party contenders accounted for only 5.3 percent of the vote (https://ballotpedia.org/California_gubernatorial_election,_2010) the last time California didn’t limit the gubernatorial choices to two candidates—Republican Meg Whitman still losing by nearly 13 points. But in 2002, four third-party candidates received a collective 10.3 percent of the November vote (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2002-general/ssov/gov-sum.pdf)—one of the reasons Republican Bill Simon lost by only five points.
About that 2002 election in California: For the first time ever (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/California-GOP-trying-to-make-sense-of-Democrats-2774055.php), Democrats won every statewide constitutional office, maintained their legislature dominance, and picked up a congressional seat. And 2026 likely offers more of the same—maybe more congressional pickups if the Proposition 50 gerrymander pans out.
California political outcomes seem little different nearly a quarter of a century later: talk about a long squeeze.

WWW.LHC.CA.GOVLITTLE HOOVER COMMISSIONFact Sheet: Addressing Weaknesses in
California’s Recall System
Contact: LittleHoover@lhc.ca.gov
The attempted recall of Governor Gavin
Newsom, which produced California’s second
gubernatorial recall election in less than 20
years, focused attention on the recall process
and on whether that system requires reform.
As California’s independent oversight agency,
the Little Hoover Commission launched a
study in 2021-2022 to consider whether
the state’s system for recalling state office-
holders should be changed, and if so, how.
The Commission concluded that the recall
system should be retained, both because it
is substantively valuable—voters should be
able to fire an elected official mid-term—and
because it is overwhelmingly popular with
voters.
Yet substantial changes are needed in
California’s recall process. Current recall
procedures breed the possibility of an
undemocratic outcome, since they allow a
replacement candidate to win office while
receiving fewer votes than the incumbent.
There is also concern that the recall is subject
to potential overuse or abuse.
In its 2022 report, Reforming the Recall, the
Commission recommends that California make two
key changes to its recall system:
◊ Adjust the signature requirement for recalling
statewide office-holders from 12 percent of
the vote in the last election for the office to 10
percent of registered voters, thereby increasing
the number of signatures necessary to initiate
a recall election and creating a more stable
signature threshold.
◊ Replace the existing two-part recall ballot with
a “snap” special election in which the official
targeted for recall is placed on the ballot with all
replacement candidates. This would ensure that
no official is recalled and replaced by a successor
who receives fewer votes.
The Commission also identified several smaller,
procedural changes that would give elections officials
more time to administer elections and provide
greater clarity around the recall process:
◊ Extend the timeframe for conducting recall
elections to no less than 88 days and no more
than 125 days from certification of the recall
petition as sufficient.
◊ Prohibit the initiation of recall proceedings
against state office-holders during the first 90
days and the last six months of their term in
office.
◊ Review recall replacement procedures to
determine which nomination standard is most
appropriate for replacement candidates, and
establish in statute which one ought to be used.
These steps will strengthen the recall system by
improving administration of the recall and better
balancing voters’ right to recall officials with
protection for electoral integrity and democratic
principles.
ADDITIONAL IMPLEMENTATION
◊ SCA 3 (Allen), 2020: Would have eliminated the
first recall ballot question and automatically
placed the official subject to recall on the ballot
as a candidate for the office.
Last updated: January 2023

Proposition 5: Will California’s Boa Constrictor Strike Again?
One seemingly innocent ballot initiative which would change California’s recall process—if voters approve it, hasta la vista, future governators (https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/november-17/the-terminator-becomes-the-governator-of-california)!—fits into a pattern of repeat efforts to guarantee that the Golden State remains under one-party, one-mentality dominance.
Thursday, October 8, 2026
5
min read
By:
Bill Whalen (https://www.hoover.org/profiles/bill-whalen) ,
Proposition 5: Will California’s Boa Constrictor Strike Again?
By:
Bill Whalen (https://www.hoover.org/profiles/bill-whalen)

Hoover Daily Report (https://www.hoover.org/publications/daily-report)

California Decides
One doesn’t need a degree in ophiology (https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/ophiology) to know that some boas achieve their goals not by venom but instead by slowly constricting their prey’s circulatory system until vital organs shut down.
At least, that’s one way to explain how one political party has dominated the California landscape this century: for the better part of the last two decades, a slow but steady constriction of the loyal opposition’s ability to affect political and policy outcomes.
Case in point: this year’s Proposition 5 (https://www.hoover.org/proposition-lab-proposition-5), one of fourteen measures on California’s November slate of ballot initiatives.
At first glance, Proposition 5 seems innocent enough, or so its official summary assures us: “ Under current law, voters elect replacement candidates at the same time as the recall election. This measure instead fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment.”
And how exactly would that work?
Again, the summary’s words:
“If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor becomes Governor for the remainder of the term or until a successor is elected”;
“for all other recalled officers, the office will remain vacant until filled by a subsequent special election or appointment as specified in existing law”;
“a recalled officer may be a candidate in a special election to fill the office.”
So how does this constitute yet another slow-but-certain “constriction”? Simple. Republicans have failed spectacularly at winning California statewide offices. (In this century, excluding the 2003 recall special election, only two GOP wins occurred in fifty-one runs for state constitutional and US Senate offices.) But there’s always been a back door to the governor’s office: the recall process.
Or so California learned when Arnold Schwarzenegger became the Golden State’s thirty-eighth governor by virtue of a recall election (https://www.politico.com/story/2017/10/07/schwarzenegger-elected-californias-governor-oct-7-2003-243512) — twenty-three years ago this week — that ousted the incumbent Democrat, Gray Davis. For Arnold, it was a two-month “fun run” — assuming the candidate enjoyed dropping wrecking balls on junkers (https://www.theguardian.com/world/2003/oct/04/usa.duncancampbell) to underscore his opposition to a “car tax” — that allowed the Republican contender to avoid a contentious GOP primary and prolonged questions about his conservative bona fides (https://californiahealthline.org/morning-breakout/schwarzenegger-social-positions-exhibit-differences-with-republican-party/).
But if voters approve Prop 5, that “back door” for a non-Democratic governor vanishes. As such, it’s just one more way in which a party that controls every statewide office, as well as supermajorities in both legislative chambers, maintains its dominance.
How else has the constrictor gone about its business in California?
Here are five examples, in reverse chronological order.
Proposition 50 . Yes, California Gov. Gavin Newsom will tell you that the ballot measure redrawing California’s congressional districts (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_50,_Use_of_Legislative_Congressional_Redistricting_Map_Amendment_(2025)) and approved by voters last November was in response to the Republican congressional gerrymander in Texas (https://redistricting.capitol.texas.gov/). And he’ll assure you it’s but a temporary step as it applies to congressional elections through 2030.
What Proposition 50 did, in the near term, was target five incumbent congressional Republicans (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-seats-would-democrats-gain-under-californias-mid-decade-redistricting-plan/). (One of them, Rep. Kevin Kiley, is now running as an independent (https://abc7news.com/post/california-rep-kevin-kiley-says-hes-leaving-republican-party-will-serve-independent/18699488/) in California’s less GOP-friendly 6th Congressional District, which stretches from the foothills of Placer County to Sacramento.)
But in the longer term, Proposition 50 “constricts” in this regard: By taking redistricting authority away from a nonpartisan, independent commission (https://wedrawthelines.ca.gov/about-us/) and instead allowing the Democratic-controlled Legislature to do the political cartography, it sets the precedent for future attempts to whittle away at the California GOP’s numbers in the US House of Representatives.
Universal Vote-By-Mail . Six years ago, California election officials rightly worried that voters going to polls amid a pandemic could trigger a superspreader event (https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2021/09/27/california-will-now-mail-ballots-voters-all-elections-permanent-extension-pandemic-era-practice/). The solution: Send a mail-in ballot to every registered regular voter, whether they asked for it or not.
A year later, Newsom signed 2021’s Assembly Bill 37 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220AB37) making California a permanent voter-by-mail state, tweeting in Trumpian fashion (https://x.com/GavinNewsom/status/1442573769906688001): “ BREAKING: California is now PERMANENTLY a vote-by-mail state. Because we believe in making voting EASIER and for every voice to be heard.”
What California’s governor conveniently omitted: voter-registration mathematics. Democrats in the Golden State outnumber Republicans by nearly a two-to-one margin (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ror/60day-gen-2026/historical-reg-stats.pdf) (it’s a twenty-point gap, as opposed to the eight-point divide between Republicans and Democrats that Schwarzenegger faced when running for reelection twenty years ago). In addition to the advanced degree in snake-handling, one doesn’t need a math doctorate to know that more ballots handed to registered Democrats means fewer chances of non-Democratic candidates or policies prevailing.
Primary Initiatives Banned . In every election cycle, California’s secretary of state publishes a thoughtful Voter Information Guide (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/) that’s mailed to all registered voters. In this election, the guide includes sixty-five pages of insight and arguments (both pro and con) devoted to fourteen ballot measures.
If you consider that information overload and would like to file a complaint, former Gov. Jerry Brown would be a good place to start.
In 2011, his first year back at the same job he held three decades earlier, Brown signed SB 202 (https://archive.nytimes.com/www.nytimes.com/gwire/2011/10/10/10greenwire-new-calif-ballot-law-seen-as-boon-to-liberal-i-42681.html?pagewanted=1), which banned voter-driven initiatives from future Golden State primary ballots. At the time, Brown tried to sell the measure as an act of good government—and good faith. “There are dramatically more voters at a general rather than a primary election," the governor’s signing statement read. “The idea of direct democracy is to involve as many voters as possible. This bill accomplishes that objective."
What Brown could have added: Moving all voter initiatives to the general election improved the odds of killing off right-leading ideas, as conservatives tend to have a larger presence in lower-turnout primaries.
Indeed, in the following year’s election, Brown’s move may have prevented “paycheck protection” (banning the use of union dues as political contributions to state and local candidates) from becoming the law of the land.
How so?
In 2012, paycheck protection was offered in the form of Proposition 32 (https://vigarchive.sos.ca.gov/2012/general/propositions/32/). Given the opportunity, the backers of that measure likely would have placed it on the ballot believing that it would benefit from the Republican primary calendar (Mitt Romney clinched the GOP nomination less than a week before California voted (https://www.politico.com/story/2012/05/mitt-clinches-gop-presidential-nod-076845)). Rare for California, the state witnessed a Republican enthusiasm gap. (Despite 2.1 million more registered Democrats than Republicans, the Democratic presidential candidates competing in California’s primary received only 150,000 more votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2012-primary/pdf/2012-complete-sov.pdf) than the GOP). Instead, Proposition 32 was relegated to the November ballot, where it received only 43.4 percent.

to potential overuse or abuse.
In its 2022 report, Reforming the Recall, the
Commission recommends that California make two
key changes to its recall system:
◊ Adjust the signature requirement for recalling
statewide office-holders from 12 percent of
the vote in the last election for the office to 10
percent of registered voters, thereby increasing
the number of signatures necessary to initiate
a recall election and creating a more stable
signature threshold.
◊ Replace the existing two-part recall ballot with
a “snap” special election in which the official
targeted for recall is placed on the ballot with all
replacement candidates. This would ensure that
no official is recalled and replaced by a successor
who receives fewer votes.
The Commission also identified several smaller,
procedural changes that would give elections officials
more time to administer elections and provide
greater clarity around the recall process:
◊ Extend the timeframe for conducting recall
elections to no less than 88 days and no more
than 125 days from certification of the recall
petition as sufficient.
◊ Prohibit the initiation of recall proceedings
against state office-holders during the first 90
days and the last six months of their term in
office.
◊ Review recall replacement procedures to
determine which nomination standard is most
appropriate for replacement candidates, and
establish in statute which one ought to be used.

improving administration of the recall and better
balancing voters’ right to recall officials with
protection for electoral integrity and democratic
principles.

Also let me consider: any counter to the "recalled official can run again" claim? Under current law, the recalled officer "may not be a candidate" in that recall election. Under Prop 5, they may run in the subsequent special election but cannot be appointed. Newman said he wasn't sure why that provision was there.

Important democratic analysis:
Pros of YES:
1. Fixes the "loser wins" problem: a replacement can take office with far fewer votes than the recalled official received to stay (28% in 2021 hypothetical; Schwarzenegger ~25% of total votes in 2003). Under Prop 5, a gubernatorial replacement must win a majority (top-two runoff) in the early-term case, and the Lt. Gov is a statewide-elected official with a mandate.
2. Reduces incentive for recalls used as a partisan "redo" of the previous election; recalls are extremely costly ($200M+ in 2021).
3. Aligns California with most other recall states.
4. Endorsed by nonpartisan good-government groups (LWV, Common Cause), Secretary of State, and McClatchy editorial board, LA Times columnists.

Cons of YES (i.e., reasons to vote NO):
1. Removes voters' direct say in choosing a replacement; transfers power to the governor (appointments for statewide constitutional officers) and to the Lt. Governor (automatic succession, possibly for up to ~2 years without any election).
2. Creates a perverse incentive: the Lt. Governor, typically the governor's same-party ally/rival, gains the governorship if a recall succeeds — potentially rewarding intra-party sabotage; also, a recall becomes a way for the same party/administration to stay in power, blunting the accountability purpose.
3. Recalled officials may run in the special election to reclaim their seat (removes a constitutional ban), which can nullify the recall's effect and could lead to endless cycles and costs. Even the author couldn't justify it.
4. Leaves districts unrepresented for months; extra special elections cost millions; net fiscal effect unknown.
5. Process/politics: authored by a recalled lawmaker, passed with almost no Republican support, no money raised by either side, and it doesn't address the real problem (low signature threshold / no grounds requirement) that the Little Hoover Commission identified. The Commission recommended a "snap election" with the incumbent on the ballot, which preserves voter choice AND majority rule — a cleaner fix. Prop 5 rejects that approach.
6. Polls show majority opposition across all partisan groups (Democrats 40% yes in Sept).

Weighing: The core flaw in the current system (plurality replacement) is real, but Prop 5's fix substitutes a system where the replacement is chosen by politicians (governor appointment) or by automatic succession (Lt. Gov), which is arguably less democratic than voters choosing on the same ballot. And it lets recalled officials immediately run to get their job back. And it doesn't address the underlying abuse issue (signature threshold). The Little Hoover Commission's recommended alternative preserves voter choice with majority rule.

Also, there's a serious concern with the gubernatorial provision: if a governor is recalled in the last two years, the Lt. Gov serves the rest of the term — up to nearly 2+ years — without any election. That means a majority vote to recall effectively installs a different person from the same ticket whom no one voted to be governor, and voters have no say. In 2003, under Prop 5 rules, Cruz Bustamante would have been governor (well, he would have been — but under Prop 5's actual text, if Davis had been recalled in Oct 2003, that's in the first two years of his second term? Davis's second term started Jan 2003, so the recall in Oct 2003 would be within the first two years — a special election would have been held with the next statewide primary (March 2004), requiring a majority. So Bustamante would serve ~5 months, then a majority-runoff election. That's arguably more legitimate than Schwarzenegger's 48.6% plurality of replacement votes (25% of total). Hmm, so Prop 5 in that case would have produced a majority-elected governor by mid-2004.

But note the counterfactual: many people would say Schwarzenegger winning was the democratic outcome since he got the most votes among replacement candidates and the recall passed by a majority.

There's a genuine normative tension: is it more democratic to have a plurality winner chosen immediately by all voters, or a majority winner chosen months later, with an interim succession by an official elected statewide on the same ticket?

Consider also the incentive effects: Under Prop 5, a recall of the governor would result in the Lt. Governor (same party, usually) taking over. That dramatically reduces the partisan stakes of recalls (a plus for reducing frivolous recalls, per supporters) but also means that a recall could no longer produce a change in the direction of government (a minus for accountability).

Another point: for legislative recalls, Prop 5 keeps a special election — voters still choose the replacement, just later, and the recalled member can run again. This means a recall of a legislator becomes potentially meaningless: they get recalled, then run right back in a special election 4 months later, likely winning again in the same district. That seriously weakens the recall as a tool. Actually that's a big deal — the recall of legislators is the most common use (9 of 11 recalls). Under Prop 5, a recalled legislator can immediately run to reclaim the seat. That undermines the whole purpose. Supporters say it's just consistent with the fact they can run in the next regular election anyway. But the timing matters: the recall just happened; a special election months later with the same electorate could easily return the same person, wasting millions.

Hmm, but also note: it could be argued that allowing the recalled official to run is fair, because under the "snap election" model recommended by Little Hoover the incumbent runs too. But in a snap election the incumbent runs at the same time as the recall decision; voters choose between them. Under Prop 5, voters first remove the official, then the official can run again to reclaim the seat. That's a strange sequence.

Now, the question is which way to recommend. Let me weigh the balance of credible, nonpartisan analysis:
- SF Chronicle editorial board (leans progressive): NO, because of the recalled-official-runs-again flaw and failure to address root causes.
- Mercury News/East Bay Times: NO.
- LA Daily News: NO.
- San Diego Union-Tribune: NO.
- Daily Bulletin: NO.
- Sacramento Bee opinion team: NO (per that endorsement list) — though McClatchy California editorial board: YES. Conflicting.
- LA Times: no editorial board position found (as of Sept 30); columnists Barabak and Skelton: YES.
- Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn: NO. Reform California: NO. CA Republican Party: NO.
- LWV, Common Cause, CA Democratic Party, Labor Federation: YES.

Polls: majority opposed (52-45 in Oct PPIC; 59-35 in Sept).

Given that a majority of independent editorial analyses say no, and the measure has genuine defects (transfers replacement power to politicians, allows recalled officials to run to reclaim the seat, leaves vacancies/unrepresented districts, doesn't fix the underlying low signature threshold, and creates an unratified succession for the Lt. Gov potentially for up to 2 years), I lean toward "no."

But let me double check a couple of things:
1. Does Prop 5 really allow the recalled officer to run in the special election? The text: Sec. 15(c) amended: "If the majority vote on the question is to recall, the officer is removed and [strikeout: if there is a candidate, the candidate who receives a plurality is the successor. The officer may not be a candidate, nor shall there be any candidacy for an office filled pursuant to subdivision (d) of Section 16 of Article VI.] and the office shall be vacant. The vacancy shall be filled in accordance with this Constitution and statute, provided that the officer who was the subject of the recall election shall not be appointed to fill the vacancy in that office."

Yes — the ban on the recalled officer being a candidate is deleted; only appointment is barred. So the recalled officer may run in the special election. Confirmed by title/summary and multiple sources.

2. For statewide officers other than governor (e.g., AG, SOS, Treasurer, Controller, Insurance Commissioner, Lt Gov): governor appoints a replacement. Wait — for the recalled governor, the Lt. Gov succeeds. For a recalled Lt. Governor, the governor appoints. And per amended Sec 17 of Article II: if recall of Governor or SOS is initiated, recall duties performed by SOS or Controller respectively (removing Lt. Gov from the chain for governor recall duties since Lt. Gov now has an interest). Good — that addresses a conflict of interest in administering the recall. Interesting detail: under Prop 5, if the governor is recalled, the SOS (not Lt Gov) handles recall duties. And if both are recalled, the Controller. That's a sensible fix.

3. Judges: Article VI Sec 16(d) covers Supreme Court justices... the strikeout mentions "nor shall there be any candidacy for an office filled pursuant to subdivision (d) of Section 16 of Article VI" — that's about appellate judges being appointed. So Prop 5 removes that too, but it's moot.

Now, is there a stronger case for YES? The main democratic principle: replacement should have majority support. Under Prop 5 for governor: either Lt. Gov (elected statewide, though as part of a ticket and for a different office) or a majority-winner special election. For legislators: special election (top-two, majority winner in general). For other statewide: gubernatorial appointment (no voter input at all — worse than current plurality vote). Hmm, for those offices (AG, Treasurer, etc.), current law lets voters choose the replacement by plurality; Prop 5 lets the governor appoint. That's clearly less democratic for those offices, though consistent with existing vacancy law (death/resignation). Recalls of those offices are extremely rare (never happened).

The realistic impact is mostly on gubernatorial and legislative recalls. For gubernatorial: Prop 5 arguably improves legitimacy (majority requirement) but eliminates voters' immediate choice and can hand the office to the Lt. Gov for up to 2 years without any election. For legislative: voters still choose, but months later, with an extra election cost, and the recalled member can run again.

Also consider: Prop 5 could increase the *frequency* of partisan recall attempts? No — supporters argue it decreases incentive. Opponents argue it discourages recalls entirely (which could be seen as good or bad).

One more consideration: the "no election at all" scenario for a late-term gubernatorial recall. Suppose a governor is recalled in month 40 of a 48-month term; the Lt. Gov serves 8 months. That's fine. But suppose recalled at month 26 (just after the "first two years" cut and after nomination period closes) — the Lt. Gov serves ~22 months without any election. That's a meaningful democratic deficit: voters removed a governor and got an unelected-by-them replacement for nearly two years. Under current law they'd elect someone immediately. That's the biggest downside.

Overall, on balance, I think "no" is the better answer: the measure's flaws (politicians choose replacements; recalled officials can immediately run to reclaim their seats; potential long unratified successions; failure to address the actual root problem of easy qualification; partisan crafting) outweigh the genuine but narrow benefit of preventing plurality replacements — especially since a better reform (Little Hoover Commission's snap election) exists that preserves voter choice and requires majority support.

Yes — the ban on the recalled officer being a candidate is deleted; only appointment is barred. So the recalled officer may run in the special election. Confirmed by title/summary and multiple sources.

2. For statewide officers other than governor (e.g., AG, SOS, Treasurer, Controller, Insurance Commissioner, Lt Gov): governor appoints a replacement. Wait — for the recalled governor, the Lt. Gov succeeds. For a recalled Lt. Governor, the governor appoints. And per amended Sec 17 of Article II: if recall of Governor or SOS is initiated, recall duties performed by SOS or Controller respectively (removing Lt. Gov from the chain for governor recall duties since Lt. Gov now has an interest). Good — that addresses a conflict of interest in administering the recall. Interesting detail: under Prop 5, if the governor is recalled, the SOS (not Lt Gov) handles recall duties. And if both are recalled, the Controller. That's a sensible fix.

3. Judges: Article VI Sec 16(d) covers Supreme Court justices... the strikeout mentions "nor shall there be any candidacy for an office filled pursuant to subdivision (d) of Section 16 of Article VI" — that's about appellate judges being appointed. So Prop 5 removes that too, but it's moot.

Now, is there a stronger case for YES? The main democratic principle: replacement should have majority support. Under Prop 5 for governor: either Lt. Gov (elected statewide, though as part of a ticket and for a different office) or a majority-winner special election. For legislators: special election (top-two, majority winner in general). For other statewide: gubernatorial appointment (no voter input at all — worse than current plurality vote). Hmm, for those offices (AG, Treasurer, etc.), current law lets voters choose the replacement by plurality; Prop 5 lets the governor appoint. That's clearly less democratic for those offices, though consistent with existing vacancy law (death/resignation). Recalls of those offices are extremely rare (never happened).

The realistic impact is mostly on gubernatorial and legislative recalls. For gubernatorial: Prop 5 arguably improves legitimacy (majority requirement) but eliminates voters' immediate choice and can hand the office to the Lt. Gov for up to 2 years without any election. For legislative: voters still choose, but months later, with an extra election cost, and the recalled member can run again.

Also consider: Prop 5 could increase the *frequency* of partisan recall attempts? No — supporters argue it decreases incentive. Opponents argue it discourages recalls entirely (which could be seen as good or bad).

One more consideration: the "no election at all" scenario for a late-term gubernatorial recall. Suppose a governor is recalled in month 40 of a 48-month term; the Lt. Gov serves 8 months. That's fine. But suppose recalled at month 26 (just after the "first two years" cut and after nomination period closes) — the Lt. Gov serves ~22 months without any election. That's a meaningful democratic deficit: voters removed a governor and got an unelected-by-them replacement for nearly two years. Under current law they'd elect someone immediately. That's the biggest downside.

Overall, on balance, I think "no" is the better answer: the measure's flaws (politicians choose replacements; recalled officials can immediately run to reclaim their seats; potential long unratified successions; failure to address the actual root problem of easy qualification; partisan crafting) outweigh the genuine but narrow benefit of preventing plurality replacements — especially since a better reform (Little Hoover Commission's snap election) exists that preserves voter choice and requires majority support.

Let me do a bit more verification: check the Daily News editorial and San Diego Union-Tribune reasoning, and check whether there's any latest poll or notable late endorsement shifting. Also check whether the election results are in (just to know context). Let me also check the League of Women Voters Easy Voter Guide for their reasoning.

Actually, let me also check for a "Fullerton Observer" piece (pro) and any pro-5 op-eds from good-government perspectives, to steelman yes.

By The Editorial Board (https://www.dailynews.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)
PUBLISHED: August 12, 2026 at 3:19 PM PDT | UPDATED: August 28, 2026 at 11:16 AM PDT
