Here’s how the current process works:
To recall a statewide official, proponents must gather signatures totaling at least 12% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the prior election. For the Newsom recall, that threshold was 1.3 million signatures (https://admin.cdn.sos.ca.gov/elections/ccrov/2025/march/25024ra.pdf). To recall members of the state Assembly and Senate, the minimum number of signatures is 20% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the last election — for Newman’s recall, that threshold was about 63,600 signatures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2018-news-releases-and-advisories/recall-signatures-senate-district-29-certified).
Once a recall qualifies, voters then receive a ballot with two questions — one, should this official be recalled, and two, who should replace them? — and a list of replacement candidates. If a simple majority votes in favor of the recall, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes wins — even if that candidate only gets a fraction of the votes against the recall.
The two-question setup is confusing — only six other states use it (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials). And permitting someone to be elected without majority support is undemocratic. Furthermore, given the distraction and price of recalls — Newsom’s cost about $200 million during (https://apnews.com/article/elections-california-legislature-gavin-newsom-state-legislature-f8b78745cc5376dc4836d914352f2116) the most fraught moments of the pandemic — they should be reserved for cases of serious misconduct or abject unfitness, not petty grievances.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Even though only 11 recalls of state-level officials have qualified for the ballot since 1913, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), California could benefit from raising the bar. Its signature-gathering threshold is among the lowest in the nation (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/Report266.pdf).
But Prop 5 doesn’t grapple with this issue.
Instead, it would eliminate the second question from the recall ballot, meaning voters would decide only whether the official should be removed.
If a majority says yes, one of three things would happen:
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would automatically step into the role. If the recall happens in the first half of a governor’s four-year term before the nomination period ends for the next statewide election, the lieutenant governor would serve until that election takes place and voters choose the next governor. But if the recall happens after that point, the lieutenant governor would finish the rest of the governor’s term.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
If another statewide official — such as the lieutenant governor, attorney general or secretary of state — is recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement. The governor already follows this process for statewide officials who die, resign or accept a different job.
And if a member of the state Legislature is recalled, the governor would call a special election for their replacement — mirroring the existing process for a lawmaker who dies, resigns or takes a different job. As the Legislative Analyst’s office notes (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), if this special election couldn’t be consolidated with an already scheduled election, it could cost state and local election officials “millions of dollars” to administer.
Newman argued to us that eliminating the second question reduces “partisan games” and prevents candidates with minority support from winning elections.
We agree that the second question is problematic and we might support its removal in isolation. But Prop 5 contains a completely unnecessary provision that permits recalled officials to run in the very special election designed to replace them — overturning a ban in the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-15/).
This is particularly egregious because incumbents fighting recall attempts can generally raise unlimited funds from donors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=85315.&lawCode=GOV). Although state law prohibits that money from being used for other campaigns, a recalled official in a special election is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received from wealthy special interests.

Newman himself couldn’t explain why Prop 5 contains that provision.
“I’m honestly not sure,” he said. “It wouldn’t pain me if it wasn’t there.”

But it is there. And the inability or unwillingness of lawmakers to put forth a simple, clean reform effort is reason enough for voters to reject this measure.
California’s recall process can certainly be improved, but the problem isn’t so dire that voters need to accept Prop 5’s glaring flaw.

When California Governor Gray Davis was the subject of a recall effort in 2003, he said in a televised speech (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-20-me-davis20-story.htmlhttps:/www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-20-me-davis20-story.html) at UCLA that he thought the recall would damage “the very fabric of our democracy.”
Elected officials may not like to see accountability arrive earlier than expected, but that doesn’t make Californians’ recall powers a threat to democracy.
While Proposition 5 doesn’t attack the people’s ability to hold a recall election, it does tinker with how a replacement candidate is selected.

Endorsement: Voters should support the Measure M bond to fix Gilroy schools (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-voters-should-support-the-measure-m-bond-to-fix-gilroy-schools/)
We urge voters to reject it.
Proposition 5 would eliminate the election of a replacement candidate on the same ballot as a recall. Currently a recall ballot has two questions: 1) Should the elected official be removed, and 2) Choose a candidate to replace that official if the recall is successful.
The measure would remove question 2, eliminating the simultaneous election for a replacement. Instead, if a state official other than a governor was recalled, the office would become vacant and would be filled by special election or appointment, according to existing law. If a governor was recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over and serve until the end of the term or until a special election could be held, depending on timing.
Under current law, a recalled official is barred from running as a replacement candidate in the special election to fill the seat. Proposition 5 changes that as well. In a special election to replace a recalled official, the recalled official could be on the ballot.
These changes turn a process to remove officials from power into a cynical blueprint to keep power in the hands of the same officials. It makes a mockery of the recall, which was designed to empower voters to remove and immediately replace an officeholder for any reason, whether the officeholder thinks the reason is sufficient or not.
Rejecting Proposition 5 is also about preserving the state’s ability to empower unique and independent political voices.
Under current rules, officials who are recalled are succeeded by the candidate seeking that official’s job who gets the most votes at the same time as the recall. This process is why Arnold Schwarzenegger was able to quickly replace the deeply unpopular Davis.
Nearly one million more Californians voted to recall Davis than to retain him, and the Republican Schwarzenegger won a plurality of the replacement vote after running as a pro-business social liberal who wanted the state to lead the global response (https://www.kqed.org/science/1931206/californias-a-team-on-climate-moonbeam-and-the-governator) to climate change.
But if Proposition 5 had been in place, Davis would have been succeeded by Lt. Gov. Cruz Bustamante. He was an uninspiring but mostly baggage-free politician who would have likely been the favorite in a subsequent regular or special election in California to finish Davis’ term, even against Schwarzenegger.
Changing the California Constitution in a way that creates even bigger obstacles to electing independent-minded candidates — while stripping the people of their primary tool of accountability — is a bad idea.
Reject Proposition 5.

Proposition 5 : Change how recalled state officials are replaced
Published September 29, 2026 · Updated November 2, 2026
Proposition 5 would remove the second question from state recall elections, the one asking who should replace the official if recalled. If a Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would become Governor, either for the rest of the term or until voters elect a new Governor, depending on timing. Other recalled offices would be filled the way vacancies are filled now: a special election for legislators and appointment by the Governor for most other offices.
Summary by CityHallPass , not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: California Official Voter Information Guide: Proposition 5 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/).
Results
Polls close at 8 p.m. Pacific on Nov. 3. First results appear here after that.
At a glance
Proposition 5
What changes State recall ballots would ask only whether to remove the official; no replacement candidates
Who fills a recalled Governor's seat The Lieutenant Governor, for the rest of the term or until a special election, depending on timing
Vote needed Simple majority
Legislature's vote Senate 32-8, Assembly 59-17 (August 2024)
Money No committee primarily formed for or against it. Against: $40,500 in outside spending by Reform California (shared with other props)
Latest public poll PPIC, Oct. 16-22: 45% yes, 52% no (likely voters)
Each figure is sourced in the sections below.
Details and source links: Polls , Money for and against , The details , How it got on the ballot , What would change , Sources .
What does a yes vote on Proposition 5 mean?
Recall elections would no longer include a question about who should fill the vacancy. Instead, vacancies typically would be filled through special elections or appointments, depending on the office and timing.
What does a no vote on Proposition 5 mean?
Voters would continue to be asked who should fill the vacancy as part of recall elections.
What would Proposition 5 cost?
The Legislative Analyst says the net effect is unknown. Separate special elections could cost millions of dollars each, while dropping replacement candidates from recall ballots could save millions. The Analyst says these costs or savings would be rare and depend on which office is recalled.
What it means for the City of LA
Proposition 5 covers only state officers: the Governor, other statewide officials, legislators and certain judges. Recalls of the Mayor, City Council members and other City officials follow the City Charter, which puts the recall question and the election of a successor on the same ballot; Proposition 5 does not change that. City residents would still vote in any state recall, and Los Angeles County's cost for the 2021 Governor recall was $52.9 million.
The details
Official title Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Type Legislative constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by the Legislature (SCA 1, Resolution Chapter 204, Statutes of 2024)
Votes needed to pass Simple majority (more than 50% yes) of votes cast statewide. Under the State Constitution (Article XVIII, Section 4), an amendment takes effect if "approved by a majority of votes cast thereon."
The question on your ballot
Under current law, voters elect replacement candidates at the same time as the recall election. This measure instead fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment. Fiscal Impact: Net fiscal effect unknown. In the event of a recall, savings or costs of millions of dollars to administer the election depending on the office recalled. Supporters: None submitted Opponents: None submitted
This is not the Proposition 5 on the November 5, 2024 ballot, the measure on local bonds for affordable housing and infrastructure, which failed with 45.0% voting yes (Secretary of State, November 2024 Statement of Vote (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2024-general/sov/59-state-ballot-measures.pdf)).
What would change
Today If Proposition 5 passes
Recall ballot Two questions: remove the official, and who replaces them if removed (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm)) One question: remove the official or not (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm))
Who takes office after a recall The replacement candidate with the most votes, even without a majority (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm)) The office becomes vacant and is filled under existing vacancy rules (text, Art. II, Sec. 15(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
Recalled Governor Replaced by the top replacement candidate The Lieutenant Governor becomes Governor. If the recall comes before the nomination period closes for the next statewide election in the first two years of the term, a special election is held with the next statewide primary, and a runoff at the general election if no one gets a majority. Otherwise the Lieutenant Governor serves out the term (text, Art. V, Sec. 10(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
Recalled legislator Replaced by the top replacement candidate Seat filled by a special election called by the Governor (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm))
Other recalled state officers (e.g. Attorney General) Replaced by the top replacement candidate Governor appoints a replacement under existing vacancy rules (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm))
Can the recalled official run again? May not be a candidate to replace themselves (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf)) May run in the later special election, but may not be appointed to the seat (title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/title-summary.htm); text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
The rules for qualifying a recall, such as signature counts and deadlines, do not change. A recall election must still be held 60 to 80 days after signatures are certified, or within 180 days if combined with a regular election (text, Art. II, Sec. 15 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
What it means for the City of Los Angeles
City recalls are not affected. Proposition 5 amends only Sections 15 and 17 of Article II and Section 10 of Article V of the State Constitution, which cover state officers (SCA 1 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1); LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm)). Recalls of City officials follow the City Charter. When a City recall petition qualifies, the Council calls an election on whether to recall the officer “and if recalled, for the election of his or her successor” (City Clerk petition handbook, p. 21, citing Charter sec. 432 (https://clerk.lacity.gov/sites/g/files/wph1491/files/2021-03/lacityp_023253.pdf#page=21)). That two-part City process stays the same.
City voters and state recalls. City residents vote in any statewide recall and in recalls of legislators who represent them. In the 2021 Governor recall, Los Angeles County voters opposed removal 70.8% to 29.2% (Statement of Vote, recall question (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/16-question.pdf)).
Election costs. County election offices run state recalls. Los Angeles County reported $52,920,735 in costs for the 2021 recall, against a state allocation of $59,793,000 (Secretary of State cost report (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/statewide-elections/2021-recall/report-to-legislature.pdf)). The Analyst says Proposition 5 could raise or lower future recall costs and that the split between the state and counties “would depend on future decisions by the Legislature” (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm)).
We found no City Council or City Clerk position on Proposition 5 as of Sept. 30, 2026.
How it got on the ballot
A constitutional amendment written by the Legislature needs a two-thirds vote of each house (SCA 1 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)).
Jan. 30, 2023: Sen. Josh Newman introduced SCA 1. Assemblymember Isaac Bryan was the principal coauthor (SCA 1 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1); SCA 1 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)).
Feb. 1, 2024: The Senate adopted it 31-7 (SCA 1 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)).
Aug. 30-31, 2024: The Assembly adopted the amended version 59-17 and the Senate agreed 32-8 (SCA 1 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)). The Senate no votes were Alvarado-Gil, Dahle, Grove, Jones, Nguyen, Niello, Ochoa Bogh and Seyarto.
Sept. 10, 2024: Filed with the Secretary of State as Resolution Chapter 204 (SCA 1 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)). It appears on the Nov. 3, 2026 ballot (SOS voter guide (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/)).
The 2018 recall of the measure’s author. Newman was recalled from the 29th Senate District in 2018, and Republican Ling Ling Chang was elected his successor on the same ballot (Secretary of State recall history (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/06-ca-recall-history.pdf)). The Daily News reports the recall passed 58% to 42% after Newman voted for a gas tax increase in 2017, and that he won the seat back in 2020 (Daily News (https://www.dailynews.com/2026/08/12/endorsement-vote-no-on-proposition-5-an-attack-on-californias-recall-power/)). The Sacramento Bee reports Chang won with just under 34% of the vote (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/proposition-5-could-change-california-s-recall-elections-here-is-our-endorsement-opinion/ar-AA2cxbHa)).
Why the vote threshold is a simple majority. A constitutional amendment “if approved by a majority of votes cast thereon, takes effect” (Cal. Const. art. XVIII, sec. 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII)).
Recall history. Since 1913, 11 state recalls have qualified for the ballot, nine against legislators and two against Governors, and six officials were removed (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm); Secretary of State recall history (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/06-ca-recall-history.pdf)). Two of the qualified recalls, both in 1994, targeted Los Angeles County legislators: Sen. David Roberti, who kept his seat, and Assemblyman Paul Horcher, who was removed (Secretary of State recall history (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/06-ca-recall-history.pdf)).
What each side says
In the state voter guide. Arguments are the authors’ opinions and are not checked for accuracy by any official agency (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/arguments-rebuttals.htm)). No supporters or opponents were listed on the ballot label (ballot label (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/)).
Argument in favor, signed by Lorrel Plimier of the League of Women Voters of California, Darius L. Kemp of California Common Cause and former FPPC chair Dan Schnur (argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
The two linked questions are “a dangerous loophole”: an official can be removed by a narrow majority and replaced by someone with “far less than 50%.”
The 2021 recall “lost by nearly the same number of votes that the Governor won the regular election with” and cost “more than $200 million.”
Had the 2021 recall succeeded, the leading replacement would have taken office “with support from only about 28% of all recall voters.”
“In most states with recalls, vacancies are already filled by succession or a separate election.”
Argument against, signed by Senate Minority Leader Brian W. Jones and Assemblymember Joe Patterson (argument against (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
It takes away voters’ power to choose a replacement. In many cases, it says, politicians rather than voters would choose who fills the vacancy.
Seats could sit vacant until “another costly election.”
The recalled official could run in the next election.
The measure’s author was recalled by voters after he voted to raise gas taxes.
Outside the guide.
Carl DeMaio, who led the 2017-18 Newman recall, told the Sacramento Bee editorial board that politicians facing a recall could say “you won’t be represented for 12 months” (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/proposition-5-could-change-california-s-recall-elections-here-is-our-endorsement-opinion/ar-AA2cxbHa)).
Newman told the Bee: “So I got more votes by way of ‘no, don’t kick him out,’ than she got by ‘yes, please put her in’” (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/proposition-5-could-change-california-s-recall-elections-here-is-our-endorsement-opinion/ar-AA2cxbHa)).
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association says the measure “makes a mockery of the recall process” (HJTA 2026 voting guide (https://www.hjta.org/2026votingguide/)).
Checking the main factual claims against official records.
Claim Who makes it What the records show
The 2021 recall cost more than $200 million Yes campaign The Secretary of State reported a total cost of $200,241,680: $174,059,031.11 for counties and $26,182,649.08 for the state (cost report (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/statewide-elections/2021-recall/report-to-legislature.pdf)).
The 2021 recall lost by about the margin Newsom won by in 2018 Yes campaign Recall question: 38.1% yes, 61.9% no (Statement of Vote, 2021 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/16-question.pdf)). 2018 Governor: Newsom 61.9%, John Cox 38.1% (Statement of Vote, 2018 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2018-general/sov/07-summary.pdf)).
The leading replacement would have won with about 28% of recall voters Yes campaign Larry Elder led with 3,563,867 votes, 48.4% of replacement votes (Statement of Vote, replacement candidates (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/20-replacement-candidates.pdf)). That is 27.8% of the 12,838,565 votes cast on the recall question (our calculation).
Politicians would choose the replacement No campaign True for statewide offices other than Governor and Lieutenant Governor succession: the Governor appoints. Legislative seats go to a special election, and a recalled Governor is succeeded by the elected Lieutenant Governor (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm)).
The recalled official could run again No campaign Yes, in the later special election; the official could not be appointed (title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/title-summary.htm)).
Special elections cost more No campaign The Analyst says a standalone special election “could be millions of dollars,” and that dropping the second question could also save millions (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm)).
We did not check the “nearly 70% of likely voters called the effort a waste” figure or the claim about recall rules in other states.
Who supports and opposes it
Supporters
League of Women Voters of California and California Common Cause, which signed the argument in favor (argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/arguments-rebuttals.htm); LWVC recommendations (https://lwvc.org/ballot-recommendations/)).
California Democratic Party (CDP positions, Aug. 2, 2026 (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf)).
California Labor Federation and State Building and Construction Trades Council, the Sacramento Bee reported (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/how-would-prop-5-change-recall-elections-if-approved-by-california-voters/ar-AA2cvWMU)).
Former Sen. Josh Newman, the author (SCA 1 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)).
Opponents
Senate Minority Leader Brian W. Jones and Assemblymember Joe Patterson, who signed the argument against (argument against (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association (HJTA 2026 voting guide (https://www.hjta.org/2026votingguide/)).
Reform California (Carl DeMaio), which reported spending against it (Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip)).
The legislators who voted no (SCA 1 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)).
Editorial boards. The Los Angeles Daily News recommends a no vote (Daily News, Aug. 12, 2026 (https://www.dailynews.com/2026/08/12/endorsement-vote-no-on-proposition-5-an-attack-on-californias-recall-power/)). The San Diego Union-Tribune also says no (San Diego Union-Tribune, Sept. 25, 2026 (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/09/25/a-vote-against-prop-5-is-a-vote-against-the-california-status-quo/)). So do the Mercury News and East Bay Times: “Reject Proposition 5” (Mercury News, Oct. 20, 2026 (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/20/endorsement-no-on-prop-5-a-bad-idea-that-protects-the-status-quo-and-silences-independent-minded-challengers/)). So does the San Francisco Chronicle. It objects to the provision that lets recalled officials run in the special election to replace them and says “the inability or unwillingness of lawmakers to put forth a simple, clean reform effort is reason enough for voters to reject this measure” (SF Chronicle, Oct. 8, 2026 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-5-recall-california-22458510.php)). Proposition 5: Preserve Voting independence

Instead, if a state official other than a governor was recalled, the office would become vacant and would be filled by special election or appointment, according to existing law.

By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 5, 2026 8:16 AM
Proposition 5 seeks to fundamentally change how California conducts recall elections for members of the Legislature and constitutional officers elected statewide.
Such elections have been rare in California.
...
If Prop.
5 is approved by state voters in November, the second question will be eliminated.
In future statewide recalls that gather enough signatures to qualify for the ballot, Californians would only vote yes or no on whether an officer should be recalled.
If a state recall of a member of the Legislature was successful, that office would remain vacant until a special election was held.
If a constitutional officer were recalled, the vacancies would be filled by the governor.
Should a future governor be recalled in the first two years of office, the Lt. Gov.
would fill the vacancy until a special election was held.
If a governor were recalled later in the term, the Lt. Gov.
would fill the vacancy until the next scheduled election.
This would be a longer process, but also one that’s more thoughtful, deliberate and — most importantly — respects the democratic norm of majority rule.

How a politician gets kicked out of office in California — and who takes their spot — could soon change.

Should this politician go?
And who should replace them?
Proposition 5 drops that second question.

...

Independent analysis
Legislative Analyst. The measure “changes the recall process to make it like the existing process for filling vacant state offices, except for the process to recall the Governor.” Net costs or savings could be millions of dollars per recall, less than 0.1% of the General Fund (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm)).

content.thinking:
Let me look at the IGS Berkeley guide, which typically provides a balanced analysis and possibly a recommendation. Also look for more academic/policy analysis on recall reform. And check whether there are other states that use a similar system.

Also key considerations:
1. Arguments for: Prevents a replacement from taking office with a minority of the vote (e.g., 28% in 2021). Aligns California with most states. Reduces cost/incentive for "recall as redo election" gambits. Lieutenant Governor is elected statewide and thus has a democratic mandate.
2. Arguments against: Removes voters' right to select replacement; potentially hands power to the governor (appointment) for other statewide offices; leaves seats vacant; the recalled official can run again in the special election (removing a constitutional ban) — which critics (including the author) find odd; partisan motivation (authored by a recalled Democrat, passed by Democratic supermajority, no Republican support); may reduce accountability and deter recalls; also creates a "succession incentive": the Lt. Gov. would benefit from the Governor being recalled — arguably creating a perverse incentive for the Lt. Gov to encourage a recall against their own party's governor. That's a real concern: under Prop 5, the Lt. Gov becomes governor if the governor is recalled. Under current law, the Lt. Gov has no such upside (in fact Cruz Bustamante ran as a replacement candidate in 2003 and lost).

Hmm, actually wait. Under Prop 5, if the governor is recalled late in term, the Lt. Gov serves the rest of the term without any election. That's a potential problem: an unpopular governor recalled in year 3.5 → Lt. Gov serves without voter ratification for up to 2 years. Under current law voters would pick a replacement immediately.

Also note: in a recall of the governor under Prop 5, if the recall happens in first two years before close of nomination period, the special election is consolidated with the statewide primary and there's a majority-winner requirement (with runoff at general). That's actually a good design — majority support. But if it happens later, no election at all.

Let's also weigh: is the measure net positive for democracy? Consider the 2003 case: Davis recalled with 55% yes; Schwarzenegger got 48.6% of replacement votes — that's a plurality of the replacement question but ~25-30% of total votes cast. Under Prop 5, Bustamante (Democrat Lt. Gov) would have become governor. Critics say that would have been less democratic since Davis was recalled by a majority. Actually the argument for Prop 5 is that a replacement should have majority support; the counter is that the current system at least lets voters choose immediately rather than leaving it to the incumbent's own party ally.

Key democratic consideration: the recall is a check on officials; if the replacement is automatically the Lt. Gov (usually same party), then the recall becomes nearly pointless as a tool for change — it removes the official but keeps the same party/administration in power. That weakens the accountability function and could deter citizens from pursuing recalls at all (as DeMaio argues). Also for legislators: recalled legislator → special election months later → the recalled official can run again (Prop 5 removes the constitutional ban), so a recalled legislator could immediately run to win back their seat, potentially rendering the recall meaningless. That's a substantial defect. Actually — under current law, Article II Section 15(c) says the recalled officer "may not be a candidate" in the recall election. Prop 5 strikes that. So a recalled official could run in the special election. This is widely criticized (SF Chronicle, Mercury News).

Hmm, but the counter-argument: a recalled official running again in a subsequent regular election is already allowed (Newman won his seat back in 2020). And preventing a recalled official from ever running is arguably too restrictive. But in a special election held months later specifically to fill their seat, it seems to undercut the recall.

Also: the governor appoints replacements for other statewide offices — that's existing vacancy law, but combined with the recall it means the governor (same party typically) picks the replacement of a recalled AG, e.g. That concentrates power.

Now let's weigh the overall evidence:
- Polls: PPIC Sept 35/59; Oct 45/52 — measure trailing, and support below majority in every partisan group including Democrats (40%). Interesting: voters broadly skeptical.

Hmm, there's confusion: the Bee's editorial board endorsed yes but the Bee's "opinion team" recommended no? The search result #8 above from sacbee "2026 Election: California Ballot proposition endorsements from our opinion team" says "❌ No on Prop 5". And result #2 says McClatchy Media's California editorial board endorsed yes. That's a contradiction — possibly two different opinion groups within McClatchy (the California editorial board vs. local opinion team). Anyway.
- Good-government groups (League of Women Voters, Common Cause) support; Howard Jarvis, Reform California, Republican legislators oppose.

Let me look for more independent academic analysis, e.g., from the IGS Berkeley guide, and any election-law scholars' views. Also check the Daily News editorial reasoning and San Diego Union-Tribune.

Let me also consider whether there's a broader consensus among political scientists about recall replacement rules. Many states (e.g., Wisconsin, Michigan?) Actually, most of the 20 recall states don't have a same-ballot replacement. California, Colorado?, Alaska, New Jersey... Let's check NCSL.

I'll fetch IGS Berkeley page and the LA Times Barabak column for a nuanced take.

Proposition 5: Statewide Officers
Proposition 5: Statewide Officers
Proposition 5: Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Recall Reform, Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment
Summary
The California Senate introduced Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (SCA) in January of 2023. As the Legislature cannot amend the California Constitution by passing legislation, the amendment must be approved by California voters. The Senate passed the bill in February of 2024 and the Assembly passed an amended version in August of 2024. The Senate agreed with the changes to the bill sending the proposed constitutional amendment to voters on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 5.
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process. Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled. If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law. Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor. If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
The financial impact would depend on how often recalls occur and which offices are involved. Costs could increase by millions of dollars when a recall creates a vacancy that requires a separate special election, particularly for legislative offices. At the same time, eliminating replacement candidates from recall ballots could save millions in some elections by reducing ballot and election-material costs. Overall, Proposition 5 could result in either costs or savings of potentially millions of dollars per recall election, although the effect would be very small compared with the state’s overall budget.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote supports changing California’s recall process so voters would decide only whether to remove an official, with the vacancy filled later under state law. A recalled official could run again, and the Lieutenant Governor would generally replace a recalled Governor.
NO: A “no” vote supports keeping the current recall process, in which voters decide whether to remove an official and simultaneously vote on who should replace that official if the recall succeeds.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that the current recall system can allow a replacement candidate to win with only a small share of the vote, particularly in low-turnout elections. They claim that Proposition 5 would make recalls more democratic and less confusing for voters while reducing opportunities to use recalls for political manipulation.
Opponents argue that voters should have the right to choose a Governor’s replacement at the time when they approve a recall. They say automatically allowing the Lieutenant Governor to take over could leave voters with a leader who shares the recalled Governor’s political views, limiting voter choice and weakening the purpose of the recall process.

That was the tab in 2021, when California held a recall election (https://www.latimes.com/topic/newsom-recall) less than a year before Gov. Gavin Newsom was set to face voters.
There was angst —the COVID-19 pandemic was raging (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-08-19/l-a-county-covid-19-deaths-top-25000-as-delta-spreads). There was anger — the lifesaving restrictions (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-12-13/california-orders-statewide-mask-order-starting-wednesday) imposed by Washington and Sacramento made daily living a chore (https://www.latimes.com/science/coronavirus-one-year-later) and drove many small businesses to the brink. Others went clear over the edge (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2020-10-29/coronavirus-pandemic-small-business-southern-california).
There was also no small amount of political opportunism at play.
The recall gave Newsom’s critics, mainly on the right, a chance to try to chase the Democrat from an office (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-08-27/recall-backers-have-california-ideas-beyond-newsom-defeat) that Republicans, under normal circumstances, stood little chance of winning.
Advertisement
In the end, the recall effort amounted to scarcely more than a partisan tantrum. The result — 61.9% voting no, 38.1% voting yes (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-09-14/recall-election-california-newsom-results) — matched the outcome of the 2018 gubernatorial race (https://www.latimes.com/politics/la-pol-ca-california-governor-race-20181106-story.html) down to the decimal. All that money and effort wasted on an election in which voters said pretty much, yep, we meant what we said. Not too long after, they gave Newsom a second term (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2022-11-08/2022-california-election-governor-newsom-dahle-results).
The plebiscite, and its pointlessness (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-09-15/newsom-california-recall-election-costly-lessons), underscored the many flaws inherent in California’s recall system. In November, voters will get a chance to remedy at least one of them, eliminating the chance a candidate could take office with just marginal support from voters.

One choice, not two
Currently, a recall election is conducted in two parts. Voters are asked whether a lawmaker should be removed and, if so, who their replacement should be. If the incumbent is ousted, whoever gets the most votes takes their place, even if they fall well shy of attaining majority support. (Which is not out of the question in a large multi-candidate field; in 2003, 135 people were on the ballot (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-27-me-recallqa27-story.html), vying to replace Gov. Gray Davis (https://www.latimes.com/la-100703recall_lat-story.html).)
Among its provisions, Proposition 5 would amend the state Constitution so that voters would be asked a simple yes-or-no question: Do you wish to recall the incumbent? If so, the lieutenant governor would serve as governor for the rest of the ousted executive’s term — unless the recall occurred during the first two years a governor was in office and before the filing deadline for the next statewide election.
In that case, a special election would be held on the same date as the next primary and a candidate receiving a majority of votes would serve out the governor’s term. If no candidate received a majority, the top-two finishers would face each other in a November runoff, with the winner taking over as governor.
Still there?
Proposition 5 has two benefits. It would save taxpayer dollars by consolidating elections and it would enhance the legitimacy and political standing of a replacement governor by ensuring he or she assumed office with at least 50% support.
But there’s still more to be done (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2022-06-23/california-recall-reform-efforts-stall).
Ending political promiscuity
California makes it way too easy to qualify a gubernatorial recall measure.
Of the 19 states that allow their governor to be booted, California is by far the most permissive. Forcing an election requires signatures reflecting just 12% of the ballots cast in the prior gubernatorial contest. In Newsom’s case, proponents needed just under 1.5 million signatures in a state with more than 22 million voters and nearly 40 million residents.
Not exactly a thundering roar.
The threshold should be higher and the reasons for kicking a governor out of office should be more serious, such as corruption, official malfeasance or conviction for a serious crime. Not just because a governor is a member of the opposite party (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2024-03-01/newsom-recall-sore-losers-are-undermining-democracy), orpeople on the losing end (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-04-13/newsom-recall-revolt-red-vs-blue-california) of an election are unhappy with the result.

The recall is a vestige of the Progressive-era good-government movement. But the process needs to be revamped (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-09-15/california-costly-confusing-gavin-newsom-recall-rethink-the-rules)to reflect today’s bad-faith political environment.
The Little Hoover Commission, California’s independent oversight agency, has recommended several changes, including raising the signature requirement and prohibiting recalls undertaken during the first 90 days and the last six months of an officeholder’s term.
Elections, it’s said, have consequences. They also have — or should have — end dates and final results that are respected, not re-litigated until the losing side gets its way.
Proposition 5 is a step in the right direction. More should follow.

The column contends that California’s gubernatorial recall process has become a costly outlet for partisan grievance, pointing to the 2021 effort against Gov. Gavin Newsom as an expensive, largely redundant re-litigation of the 2018 election rather than a meaningful exercise in accountability [5] (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/op-ed/article253864413.html) . It suggests that such recalls siphon public money and attention from governance while merely confirming outcomes voters had already endorsed [5] (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/op-ed/article253864413.html) .
The article argues that the core structural flaw in California’s recall rules is the two-question ballot, which allows voters to remove an incumbent by majority vote while simultaneously electing a replacement who may win with only a small plurality [2] (https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2022-02-13/editorial-californias-recall-rules-could-let-a-loser-win-its-time-to-change-that) [6] (https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2024-03-19/editorial-newsom-recall-still-not-fixed-undemocratic-rules) [11] (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-08-16/skelton-recall-constitutionality-newsom-california-governor) . It notes that in a crowded field this can produce a scenario where a governor receives far more votes than the successor yet still loses office, a result critics in other commentaries have labeled undemocratic and potentially unconstitutional [2] (https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2022-02-13/editorial-californias-recall-rules-could-let-a-loser-win-its-time-to-change-that) [6] (https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2024-03-19/editorial-newsom-recall-still-not-fixed-undemocratic-rules) [11] (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-08-16/skelton-recall-constitutionality-newsom-california-governor) .
Building on that critique, the piece supports Proposition 5, a legislatively referred constitutional amendment on the November 2026 ballot that would eliminate the simultaneous successor election and ask a single yes-or-no question about recalling the incumbent [4] (https://fullertonobserver.com/2026/08/15/california-proposition-5-2026-eliminating-the-successor-election-in-state-officer-recalls/) [7] (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316600442.html) [12] (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-5/) . It explains that, under the measure, a recalled governor’s seat would be filled either by the lieutenant governor for the remainder of the term or, when the recall occurs early in a term, by a special election in which the winner must secure a majority, with a runoff if necessary, thereby ensuring the replacement takes office with broader voter support [4] (https://fullertonobserver.com/2026/08/15/california-proposition-5-2026-eliminating-the-successor-election-in-state-officer-recalls/) [7] (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316600442.html) [12] (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-5/) .
The column further maintains that California’s signature threshold for initiating a gubernatorial recall—12% of votes cast in the previous governor’s race, roughly 1.5 million signatures in Newsom’s case—makes it too easy for a relatively small, motivated minority to force a statewide election [9] (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/prior-elections/statewide-election-results/2021-ca-gov-recall/newsom-recall-faqs) [10] (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article250011419.html) . It argues that the bar should be higher and that grounds for recall should be limited to serious misconduct such as corruption or criminal conviction, echoing concerns in oversight reports that the current open-ended standard invites overuse and abuse of the process [1] (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/FactSheet266.pdf) [8] (https://lhc.ca.gov/report/reforming-recall/) [10] (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article250011419.html) .
In addition, the piece suggests that the recall has drifted from its Progressive-era good-government roots into a tool for “bad actors” who can target officials they simply dislike and potentially install successors lacking majority support [1] (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/FactSheet266.pdf) [8] (https://lhc.ca.gov/report/reforming-recall/) . It cites reform recommendations from the Little Hoover Commission, which has urged changes such as raising the signature requirement and restricting recall timing, as evidence that independent watchdogs also see the existing framework as vulnerable to manipulation and in need of modernization [1] (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/FactSheet266.pdf) [8] (https://lhc.ca.gov/report/reforming-recall/) .
Different views on the topic
A law review article argues that California’s recall system is not overpowered and, in fact, functions much as its Progressive-era designers intended: as a difficult but potent “voter weapon” to menace and remove public officials when necessary [3] (https://digitalcommons.law.scu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2938&context=lawreview) . It notes that from 1911 to 2021, 179 recall petitions were filed against state officials, but only 11 qualified for the ballot and just six succeeded, a record the piece uses to contend that recalls are already rare and that fears of rampant abuse are overstated [3] (https://digitalcommons.law.scu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2938&context=lawreview) .
While sharing concerns about undemocratic outcomes, some reform advocates favor a different structural fix than Proposition 5, proposing a “snap” special recall election in which the incumbent appears on the ballot alongside all challengers rather than leaving the office temporarily vacant [8] (https://lhc.ca.gov/report/reforming-recall/) . The Little Hoover Commission, for example, recommends replacing the two-part ballot with such a system and adjusting the signature requirement to 10% of registered voters, arguing that this approach both raises the bar for launching a recall and ensures that any successor must defeat the incumbent directly in a single election [1] (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/FactSheet266.pdf) [8] (https://lhc.ca.gov/report/reforming-recall/) .
The law review piece also emphasizes the historical role of the recall as a central Progressive innovation that gives voters a direct tool to check officials between regular election cycles, and it warns that sweeping restrictions on who can initiate recalls or on permissible reasons could blunt that instrument of accountability [3] (https://digitalcommons.law.scu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2938&context=lawreview) . By stressing that recall attempts are frequently filed but rarely successful, the article suggests that the existing hurdles already filter out frivolous efforts and that tightening the rules further could unduly insulate incumbents from public pressure [3] (https://digitalcommons.law.scu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2938&context=lawreview) .

Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process.

One seemingly innocent ballot initiative which would change California’s recall process—if voters approve it, hasta la vista, future governators (https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/november-17/the-terminator-becomes-the-governator-of-california)!—fits into a pattern of repeat efforts to guarantee that the Golden State remains under one-party, one-mentality dominance.

One doesn’t need a degree in ophiology (https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/ophiology) to know that some boas achieve their goals not by venom but instead by slowly constricting their prey’s circulatory system until vital organs shut down.
At least, that’s one way to explain how one political party has dominated the California landscape this century: for the better part of the last two decades, a slow but steady constriction of the loyal opposition’s ability to affect political and policy outcomes.
Case in point: this year’s Proposition 5 (https://www.hoover.org/proposition-lab-proposition-5), one of fourteen measures on California’s November slate of ballot initiatives.
At first glance, Proposition 5 seems innocent enough, or so its official summary assures us: “ Under current law, voters elect replacement candidates at the same time as the recall election. This measure instead fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment.”
And how exactly would that work?
Again, the summary’s words:
“If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor becomes Governor for the remainder of the term or until a successor is elected”;
“for all other recalled officers, the office will remain vacant until filled by a subsequent special election or appointment as specified in existing law”;
“a recalled officer may be a candidate in a special election to fill the office.”
So how does this constitute yet another slow-but-certain “constriction”? Simple. Republicans have failed spectacularly at winning California statewide offices. (In this century, excluding the 2003 recall special election, only two GOP wins occurred in fifty-one runs for state constitutional and US Senate offices.) But there’s always been a back door to the governor’s office: the recall process.
Or so California learned when Arnold Schwarzenegger became the Golden State’s thirty-eighth governor by virtue of a recall election (https://www.politico.com/story/2017/10/07/schwarzenegger-elected-californias-governor-oct-7-2003-243512) — twenty-three years ago this week — that ousted the incumbent Democrat, Gray Davis. For Arnold, it was a two-month “fun run” — assuming the candidate enjoyed dropping wrecking balls on junkers (https://www.theguardian.com/world/2003/oct/04/usa.duncancampbell) to underscore his opposition to a “car tax” — that allowed the Republican contender to avoid a contentious GOP primary and prolonged questions about his conservative bona fides (https://californiahealthline.org/morning-breakout/schwarzenegger-social-positions-exhibit-differences-with-republican-party/).
But if voters approve Prop 5, that “back door” for a non-Democratic governor vanishes. As such, it’s just one more way in which a party that controls every statewide office, as well as supermajorities in both legislative chambers, maintains its dominance.
How else has the constrictor gone about its business in California?
Here are five examples, in reverse chronological order.
Proposition 50 . Yes, California Gov. Gavin Newsom will tell you that the ballot measure redrawing California’s congressional districts (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_50,_Use_of_Legislative_Congressional_Redistricting_Map_Amendment_(2025)) and approved by voters last November was in response to the Republican congressional gerrymander in Texas (https://redistricting.capitol.texas.gov/). And he’ll assure you it’s but a temporary step as it applies to congressional elections through 2030.
What Proposition 50 did, in the near term, was target five incumbent congressional Republicans (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-seats-would-democrats-gain-under-californias-mid-decade-redistricting-plan/). (One of them, Rep. Kevin Kiley, is now running as an independent (https://abc7news.com/post/california-rep-kevin-kiley-says-hes-leaving-republican-party-will-serve-independent/18699488/) in California’s less GOP-friendly 6th Congressional District, which stretches from the foothills of Placer County to Sacramento.)
But in the longer term, Proposition 50 “constricts” in this regard: By taking redistricting authority away from a nonpartisan, independent commission (https://wedrawthelines.ca.gov/about-us/) and instead allowing the Democratic-controlled Legislature to do the political cartography, it sets the precedent for future attempts to whittle away at the California GOP’s numbers in the US House of Representatives.
Universal Vote-By-Mail . Six years ago, California election officials rightly worried that voters going to polls amid a pandemic could trigger a superspreader event (https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2021/09/27/california-will-now-mail-ballots-voters-all-elections-permanent-extension-pandemic-era-practice/). The solution: Send a mail-in ballot to every registered regular voter, whether they asked for it or not.
A year later, Newsom signed 2021’s Assembly Bill 37 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220AB37) making California a permanent voter-by-mail state, tweeting in Trumpian fashion (https://x.com/GavinNewsom/status/1442573769906688001): “ BREAKING: California is now PERMANENTLY a vote-by-mail state. Because we believe in making voting EASIER and for every voice to be heard.”
What California’s governor conveniently omitted: voter-registration mathematics. Democrats in the Golden State outnumber Republicans by nearly a two-to-one margin (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ror/60day-gen-2026/historical-reg-stats.pdf) (it’s a twenty-point gap, as opposed to the eight-point divide between Republicans and Democrats that Schwarzenegger faced when running for reelection twenty years ago). In addition to the advanced degree in snake-handling, one doesn’t need a math doctorate to know that more ballots handed to registered Democrats means fewer chances of non-Democratic candidates or policies prevailing.
Primary Initiatives Banned . In every election cycle, California’s secretary of state publishes a thoughtful Voter Information Guide (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/) that’s mailed to all registered voters. In this election, the guide includes sixty-five pages of insight and arguments (both pro and con) devoted to fourteen ballot measures.
If you consider that information overload and would like to file a complaint, former Gov. Jerry Brown would be a good place to start.
In 2011, his first year back at the same job he held three decades earlier, Brown signed SB 202 (https://archive.nytimes.com/www.nytimes.com/gwire/2011/10/10/10greenwire-new-calif-ballot-law-seen-as-boon-to-liberal-i-42681.html?pagewanted=1), which banned voter-driven initiatives from future Golden State primary ballots. At the time, Brown tried to sell the measure as an act of good government—and good faith. “There are dramatically more voters at a general rather than a primary election," the governor’s signing statement read. “The idea of direct democracy is to involve as many voters as possible. This bill accomplishes that objective."
What Brown could have added: Moving all voter initiatives to the general election improved the odds of killing off right-leading ideas, as conservatives tend to have a larger presence in lower-turnout primaries.
Indeed, in the following year’s election, Brown’s move may have prevented “paycheck protection” (banning the use of union dues as political contributions to state and local candidates) from becoming the law of the land.
How so?
In 2012, paycheck protection was offered in the form of Proposition 32 (https://vigarchive.sos.ca.gov/2012/general/propositions/32/). Given the opportunity, the backers of that measure likely would have placed it on the ballot believing that it would benefit from the Republican primary calendar (Mitt Romney clinched the GOP nomination less than a week before California voted (https://www.politico.com/story/2012/05/mitt-clinches-gop-presidential-nod-076845)). Rare for California, the state witnessed a Republican enthusiasm gap. (Despite 2.1 million more registered Democrats than Republicans, the Democratic presidential candidates competing in California’s primary received only 150,000 more votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2012-primary/pdf/2012-complete-sov.pdf) than the GOP). Instead, Proposition 32 was relegated to the November ballot, where it received only 43.4 percent.
Despite this constricting move, right-of-center and free-market ideas can still prevail in the form of ballot initiatives—but maybe not that many initiatives if the going rate for victory is at least $200 million (https://www.sfexaminer.com/news/politics/billionaire-tax-fight-has-become-200m-battle/article_31b8898d-bb5a-4ff5-97a0-5921537adea6.html).
Majority Budgets . In the same 2010 election that returned Jerry Brown to the governor’s office, California voters sent a message to a legislature fresh off a three-month budgetary stalemate (https://www.bbc.com/news/world-us-canada-11458248) with Schwarzenegger: The next time the budget is delayed, you won’t get paid until you do your job.
Also a part of Proposition 25 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_25,_Simple_Majority_Vote_to_Enact_State_Budget_Amendment_(2010)), which made that salary-docking threat: lowering the vote requirement for each house of the legislature to pass a budget bill from two-thirds to a simple majority. (California, at the time, was one of only three states with the two-thirds requirement.)
The constriction was none too subtle. With Democrats firmly in control of the legislature when voters approved Proposition 25, but lacking supermajorities in either chamber, the constitutional tweak immediately made legislative Republicans irrelevant when charting California’s fiscal course—an irrelevancy that continues to this day.
Open Primaries . Proposition 14 wasn't California's only experiment in making democracy work to one party's advantage. Also on the ballot in November 2010 was Proposition 14 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_14,_Top-Two_Primaries_Amendment_(June_2010)), which offered a new “top two” primary system that advanced the lead two vote getters to the general election regardless of political affiliation.
Proponents of the ballot measure also talked about future primaries producing a new California politician (at the time, the political prognosticator Nate Silver predicted a future wave of New England-style moderates in the Golden State (https://web.archive.org/web/20140207043720/http:/www.fivethirtyeight.com/2009/02/land-of-thousand-liebermans.html)).
But what went overlooked at the time: Proposition 14 didn’t allow third parties access to the November ballot unless they finished first or second in the primary.
The constriction: keeping third-party candidates off the November ballot also keeps disgruntled Democrats and independents (currently breaking Democratic at a two-to-one rate (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/08s5x10r) in this year’s governor’s race) from leaving the flock.
A crippling blow it’s not. Third-party contenders accounted for only 5.3 percent of the vote (https://ballotpedia.org/California_gubernatorial_election,_2010) the last time California didn’t limit the gubernatorial choices to two candidates—Republican Meg Whitman still losing by nearly 13 points. But in 2002, four third-party candidates received a collective 10.3 percent of the November vote (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2002-general/ssov/gov-sum.pdf)—one of the reasons Republican Bill Simon lost by only five points.
About that 2002 election in California: For the first time ever (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/California-GOP-trying-to-make-sense-of-Democrats-2774055.php), Democrats won every statewide constitutional office, maintained their legislature dominance, and picked up a congressional seat. And 2026 likely offers more of the same—maybe more congressional pickups if the Proposition 50 gerrymander pans out.
California political outcomes seem little different nearly a quarter of a century later: talk about a long squeeze.

WWW.LHC.CA.GOVLITTLE HOOVER COMMISSIONFact Sheet: Addressing Weaknesses in
California’s Recall System
Contact: LittleHoover@lhc.ca.gov
The attempted recall of Governor Gavin
Newsom, which produced California’s second
gubernatorial recall election in less than 20
years, focused attention on the recall process
and on whether that system requires reform.
As California’s independent oversight agency,
the Little Hoover Commission launched a
study in 2021-2022 to consider whether
the state’s system for recalling state office-
holders should be changed, and if so, how.
The Commission concluded that the recall
system should be retained, both because it
is substantively valuable—voters should be
able to fire an elected official mid-term—and
because it is overwhelmingly popular with
voters.
Yet substantial changes are needed in
California’s recall process. Current recall
procedures breed the possibility of an
undemocratic outcome, since they allow a
replacement candidate to win office while
receiving fewer votes than the incumbent.
There is also concern that the recall is subject
to potential overuse or abuse.
In its 2022 report, Reforming the Recall, the
Commission recommends that California make two
key changes to its recall system:
◊ Adjust the signature requirement for recalling
statewide office-holders from 12 percent of
the vote in the last election for the office to 10
percent of registered voters, thereby increasing
the number of signatures necessary to initiate
a recall election and creating a more stable
signature threshold.
◊ Replace the existing two-part recall ballot with
a “snap” special election in which the official
targeted for recall is placed on the ballot with all
replacement candidates. This would ensure that
no official is recalled and replaced by a successor
who receives fewer votes.
The Commission also identified several smaller,
procedural changes that would give elections officials
more time to administer elections and provide
greater clarity around the recall process:
◊ Extend the timeframe for conducting recall
elections to no less than 88 days and no more
than 125 days from certification of the recall
petition as sufficient.
◊ Prohibit the initiation of recall proceedings
against state office-holders during the first 90
days and the last six months of their term in
office.
◊ Review recall replacement procedures to
determine which nomination standard is most
appropriate for replacement candidates, and
establish in statute which one ought to be used.
These steps will strengthen the recall system by
improving administration of the recall and better
balancing voters’ right to recall officials with
protection for electoral integrity and democratic
principles.
ADDITIONAL IMPLEMENTATION
◊ SCA 3 (Allen), 2020: Would have eliminated the
first recall ballot question and automatically
placed the official subject to recall on the ballot
as a candidate for the office.
Last updated: January 2023

Fixes the "loser wins" problem: a replacement can take office with far fewer votes than the recalled official received to stay (28% in 2021 hypothetical; Schwarzenegger ~25% of total votes in 2003). Under Prop 5, a gubernatorial replacement must win a majority (top-two runoff) in the early-term case, and the Lt. Gov is a statewide-elected official with a mandate.
2. Reduces incentive for recalls used as a partisan "redo" of the previous election; recalls are extremely costly ($200M+ in 2021).
3. Aligns California with most other recall states.
4. Endorsed by nonpartisan good-government groups (LWV, Common Cause), Secretary of State, and McClatchy editorial board, LA Times columnists.

Cons of YES (i.e., reasons to vote NO):
1. Removes voters' direct say in choosing a replacement; transfers power to the governor (appointments for statewide constitutional officers) and to the Lt. Governor (automatic succession, possibly for up to ~2 years without any election).
2. Creates a perverse incentive: the Lt. Governor, typically the governor's same-party ally/rival, gains the governorship if a recall succeeds — potentially rewarding intra-party sabotage; also, a recall becomes a way for the same party/administration to stay in power, blunting the accountability purpose.
3. Recalled officials may run in the special election to reclaim their seat (removes a constitutional ban), which can nullify the recall's effect and could lead to endless cycles and costs. Even the author couldn't justify it.
4. Leaves districts unrepresented for months; extra special elections cost millions; net fiscal effect unknown.
5. Process/politics: authored by a recalled lawmaker, passed with almost no Republican support, no money raised by either side, and it doesn't address the real problem (low signature threshold / no grounds requirement) that the Little Hoover Commission identified. The Commission recommended a "snap election" with the incumbent on the ballot, which preserves voter choice AND majority rule — a cleaner fix. Prop 5 rejects that approach.
6. Polls show majority opposition across all partisan groups (Democrats 40% yes in Sept).

Weighing: The core flaw in the current system (plurality replacement) is real, but Prop 5's fix substitutes a system where the replacement is chosen by politicians (governor appointment) or by automatic succession (Lt. Gov), which is arguably less democratic than voters choosing on the same ballot. And it lets recalled officials immediately run to get their job back. And it doesn't address the underlying abuse issue (signature threshold). The Little Hoover Commission's recommended alternative preserves voter choice with majority rule.

Also, there's a serious concern with the gubernatorial provision: if a governor is recalled in the last two years, the Lt. Gov serves the rest of the term — up to nearly 2+ years — without any election. That means a majority vote to recall effectively installs a different person from the same ticket whom no one voted to be governor, and voters have no say. In 2003, under Prop 5 rules, Cruz Bustamante would have been governor (well, he would have been — but under Prop 5's actual text, if Davis had been recalled in Oct 2003, that's in the first two years of his second term? Davis's second term started Jan 2003, so the recall in Oct 2003 would be within the first two years — a special election would have been held with the next statewide primary (March 2004), requiring a majority. So Bustamante would serve ~5 months, then a majority-runoff election. That's arguably more legitimate than Schwarzenegger's 48.6% plurality of replacement votes (25% of total). Hmm, so Prop 5 in that case would have produced a majority-elected governor by mid-2004.

But note the counterfactual: many people would say Schwarzenegger winning was the democratic outcome since he got the most votes among replacement candidates and the recall passed by a majority.

There's a genuine normative tension: is it more democratic to have a plurality winner chosen immediately by all voters, or a majority winner chosen months later, with an interim succession by an official elected statewide on the same ticket?

Consider also the incentive effects: Under Prop 5, a recall of the governor would result in the Lt. Governor (same party, usually) taking over. That dramatically reduces the partisan stakes of recalls (a plus for reducing frivolous recalls, per supporters) but also means that a recall could no longer produce a change in the direction of government (a minus for accountability).

Another point: for legislative recalls, Prop 5 keeps a special election — voters still choose the replacement, just later, and the recalled member can run again. This means a recall of a legislator becomes potentially meaningless: they get recalled, then run right back in a special election 4 months later, likely winning again in the same district. That seriously weakens the recall as a tool. Actually that's a big deal — the recall of legislators is the most common use (9 of 11 recalls). Under Prop 5, a recalled legislator can immediately run to reclaim the seat. That undermines the whole purpose. Supporters say it's just consistent with the fact they can run in the next regular election anyway. But the timing matters: the recall just happened; a special election months later with the same electorate could easily return the same person, wasting millions.

Hmm, but also note: it could be argued that allowing the recalled official to run is fair, because under the "snap election" model recommended by Little Hoover the incumbent runs too. But in a snap election the incumbent runs at the same time as the recall decision; voters choose between them. Under Prop 5, voters first remove the official, then the official can run again to reclaim the seat. That's a strange sequence.

- Mercury News/East Bay Times: NO.
- LA Daily News: NO.
- San Diego Union-Tribune: NO.
- Daily Bulletin: NO.

- Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn: NO. Reform California: NO. CA Republican Party: NO.

Polls: majority opposed (52-45 in Oct PPIC; 59-35 in Sept).

Gov potentially for up to 2 years), I lean toward "no."

But let me double check a couple of things:
1. Does Prop 5 really allow the recalled officer to run in the special election? The text: Sec. 15(c) amended: "If the majority vote on the question is to recall, the officer is removed and [strikeout: if there is a candidate, the candidate who receives a plurality is the successor. The officer may not be a candidate, nor shall there be any candidacy for an office filled pursuant to subdivision (d) of Section 16 of Article VI.] and the office shall be vacant. The vacancy shall be filled in accordance with this Constitution and statute, provided that the officer who was the subject of the recall election shall not be appointed to fill the vacancy in that office."

Yes — the ban on the recalled officer being a candidate is deleted; only appointment is barred. So the recalled officer may run in the special election. Confirmed by title/summary and multiple sources.

2. For statewide officers other than governor (e.g., AG, SOS, Treasurer, Controller, Insurance Commissioner, Lt Gov): governor appoints a replacement. Wait — for the recalled governor, the Lt. Gov succeeds. For a recalled Lt. Governor, the governor appoints. And per amended Sec 17 of Article II: if recall of Governor or SOS is initiated, recall duties performed by SOS or Controller respectively (removing Lt. Gov from the chain for governor recall duties since Lt. Gov now has an interest). Good — that addresses a conflict of interest in administering the recall. Interesting detail: under Prop 5, if the governor is recalled, the SOS (not Lt Gov) handles recall duties. And if both are recalled, the Controller. That's a sensible fix.

3. Judges: Article VI Sec 16(d) covers Supreme Court justices... the strikeout mentions "nor shall there be any candidacy for an office filled pursuant to subdivision (d) of Section 16 of Article VI" — that's about appellate judges being appointed. So Prop 5 removes that too, but it's moot.

Now, is there a stronger case for YES? The main democratic principle: replacement should have majority support. Under Prop 5 for governor: either Lt. Gov (elected statewide, though as part of a ticket and for a different office) or a majority-winner special election. For legislators: special election (top-two, majority winner in general). For other statewide: gubernatorial appointment (no voter input at all — worse than current plurality vote). Hmm, for those offices (AG, Treasurer, etc.), current law lets voters choose the replacement by plurality; Prop 5 lets the governor appoint. That's clearly less democratic for those offices, though consistent with existing vacancy law (death/resignation). Recalls of those offices are extremely rare (never happened).

The realistic impact is mostly on gubernatorial and legislative recalls. For gubernatorial: Prop 5 arguably improves legitimacy (majority requirement) but eliminates voters' immediate choice and can hand the office to the Lt. Gov for up to 2 years without any election. For legislative: voters still choose, but months later, with an extra election cost, and the recalled member can run again.

Also consider: Prop 5 could increase the *frequency* of partisan recall attempts? No — supporters argue it decreases incentive. Opponents argue it discourages recalls entirely (which could be seen as good or bad).

One more consideration: the "no election at all" scenario for a late-term gubernatorial recall. Suppose a governor is recalled in month 40 of a 48-month term; the Lt. Gov serves 8 months. That's fine. But suppose recalled at month 26 (just after the "first two years" cut and after nomination period closes) — the Lt. Gov serves ~22 months without any election. That's a meaningful democratic deficit: voters removed a governor and got an unelected-by-them replacement for nearly two years. Under current law they'd elect someone immediately. That's the biggest downside.

Overall, on balance, I think "no" is the better answer: the measure's flaws (politicians choose replacements; recalled officials can immediately run to reclaim their seats; potential long unratified successions; failure to address the actual root problem of easy qualification; partisan crafting) outweigh the genuine but narrow benefit of preventing plurality replacements — especially since a better reform (Little Hoover Commission's snap election) exists that preserves voter choice and requires majority support.
